recruits.name: Dan Okafor
recruits.backstory: Twenty-two years on a Sheffield steel floor. Heat, noise, a four-man crew and the kind of trust you can't talk about without sounding daft. Then the plant shut. Then the world ended, which he'll tell you came as less of a shock than the first one. He's a shield. That's the whole arrangement. He stands in front and the rest of you get on with it.
recruits.greeting: I'll go first. Don't thank me. It's the job and somebody has to have it.
recruits.home_note: At the drill grounds in Valley of Strength.

background_sections.before:
The floor. Shift work. A crew that went for a pint on Fridays for nine years straight.

The plant closed in 2019. He was out of work for four years and most of that is a subject he'll walk away from.
background_sections.adjustment: He stopped being idle. He'd call that the entire adjustment and he's wrong, but he's wrong in a direction that works.
background_sections.now:
Southpoint, on the Hillsbrad coast. A working town. He understands working towns.

He takes the front of whatever goes out and he's never once asked to be paid differently for it.
background_sections.forward:
A crew. Four men, long shifts, a Friday.

He's been assembling one out of whoever's in the tavern and it isn't the same and he won't say so.

His daughter was in Leeds. The lists at the hub are alphabetical and he's got to the D's about forty times.

recruits.name: Ama Boateng
recruits.backstory: There's a rule about her hours and everybody in Razor Hill knows she breaks it. Twice now the orc women have walked her back to her own cot with a hand between her shoulder blades. She was a children's nurse somewhere with four cots to a bay and an arithmetic nobody said out loud, and what she carried over wasn't the healing. It was the arithmetic. She still runs it, every time, on a world that doesn't make her.
recruits.greeting: Sit down. No, sit, I'm not asking twice, and you're dripping on a floor I've already done once today.
recruits.home_note: Set up in the infirmary tent.

background_sections.before:
Paediatric nights, four to a bay, and a ward sister who taught her to keep her voice level while her hands did something frightening. That skill looks like calm from the outside. It's something else from the inside.

She was very good. It cost her a marriage and most of her twenties, and she'd tell you the trade was obvious.
background_sections.adjustment:
The first two years aren't a subject. Nobody in Razor Hill asks.

What she'll say is this: back home there was always a form, a referral, a reason you couldn't. Here there's light in her hands and no limit at all, and for a year nothing in the world told her to stop. An orc woman whose son she'd kept breathing finally picked her up off the floor and told her.
background_sections.now:
Razor Hill. The road brings in whatever the Barrens did to people that week.

The children stopped being frightened of her a long while after the adults did. She thinks that's the correct order.
background_sections.forward:
Somebody has to be able to do this when she's out of the room. Not a student. A replacement. She's been looking for two years and turned four people down for reasons she can't put into words, and that's the problem and she knows it.

There's a notebook as well. The handwriting is appalling on purpose.

She isn't looking for anybody. Her mother died in Lagos the February before it happened. She's described that once, as the only good timing in this entire business, and then changed the subject so hard the other person apologised.

recruits.name: Silas Vance
recruits.backstory: Ask what he did before and you'll get a different answer each time, all of them port work, none of them checkable. What's true is that he reads a dock the way other people read a face. Which crate's light, which captain's lying, who's about to be robbed by the man standing next to him. He sells that at a fair price and it still faintly embarrasses him. He arrived expecting a free-for-all: no record, no reputation, nothing to live down. What he found was a frontier with sharper rules than Antwerp ever had, because out here the people who break them don't get a hearing. Took four months to understand and it reorganised him completely.
recruits.greeting: You want someone who hits things, or someone who hits things first? Different rates. I'll quote you the second and do the first. That's not a scam, that's a discount.
recruits.home_note: At the docks, leaning on a crate like he owns it.

background_sections.before:
Five years of cargo manifests and camera feeds and the dockside arrangement where everybody took a little and nobody took enough to become a problem.

He never joined in. He never reported it either. Ask him then what he believed in and he'd have changed the subject, quickly.

There's nobody he's looking for. He mentions that more often than a man who meant it would.
background_sections.adjustment: He landed delighted. He's embarrassed about that now in a way he wouldn't have predicted.
background_sections.now:
Ratchet. A port. The only shape of place he's ever been able to read properly.

There's a goblin on the middle pier paying him a retainer not to tell anyone else what he notices. Silas considers it the single most legitimate income of his life.
background_sections.forward:
A berth. Not ownership, he's not built for it. A cut, a pier, a reason to be in the same place next year.

He's never committed to anything and he's started to suspect that isn't the same as being free. He's got as far as suspecting it.

recruits.name: Rosa Delgado
recruits.backstory: Eight years guiding in Tanzania taught her that a predator isn't cruel and hunger isn't personal, and she got very tired of explaining both to people who needed the lion to mean something. The savanna didn't care about her. That was most of what she loved about it. Then she got here, where the animals think, where a quilboar runs a plan and changes the plan when it sees you, and she had to stop tracking and start anticipating. She was bad at it for a year. She hadn't been bad at anything in a decade and it nearly took her legs out from under her.
recruits.greeting: Do you have any idea what's living out here? No? Then yes. I'm coming with you.
recruits.home_note: At the treeline with her kill hung.

background_sections.before: Researchers, photographers, the occasional idiot with money, and a great deal of sitting absolutely still in the dark.
background_sections.adjustment:
A year of being outclassed by pigs. She'll put it exactly that way, to anyone, immediately.

She came out of it a better hunter than she went in and she's not grateful. That same year she found out the Arusha hub came down south of the range, which is another way of saying her mother is on the far side of a mountain that wasn't there.
background_sections.now:
The Central Barrens, close enough to savanna to hurt. Dry grass, long sightlines, big animals moving slow in the heat.

She works the Crossroads road where the hyenas have worked out what a caravan is. She can tell you what a pack's about to do four seconds before it does it. She's trying to teach that and finding it won't go into words.
background_sections.forward:
The coast. No reason. She grew up a long way from an ocean, spent her career further from one, and has decided she's owed.

After that, somewhere unmapped. She came for wild and the wild keeps turning out to have a road through it.

recruits.name: Marco Rossi
recruits.backstory: Thirty-one years a Naples locksmith, and for twenty of those the man the neighbourhood sent for when something was wrong and the authorities were worse than the problem. He settled disputes because somebody had to and because he was the only one everybody owed a favour. The Light found him already doing the work and he regards the whole business as a formality that arrived late.
recruits.greeting: I will stand here. You do what you came to do.
recruits.home_note: In the Trade Quarter, keeping the peace by the Seal.

background_sections.before:
A shop, a quarter, and a reputation he spent thirty years being careful with.

A wife, two daughters, and a grandson born in the February. He had held him four times.
background_sections.adjustment:
He looked for people to be useful to and found them in a fortnight.

Everything else he put off, and he is still putting it off, and at sixty-three he has decided that is a legitimate way to handle it.
background_sections.now:
Southshore, in the lanes behind the inn, where the town has quietly worked out who to fetch.

He fixes locks. He also fixes other things and nobody has ever asked him to.
background_sections.forward:
A quarter again. A few streets where people know to come to him.

He has about half of one in Southshore. He is counting.

recruits.name: Sophia Dias
recruits.backstory: Fourteen years a translator at the European Parliament. Simultaneous, four languages: you hold a sentence in one tongue while it finishes in another, and you get the register right as well as the words. Arcane work asks for precisely that kind of attention held precisely that long. She was better prepared for this than almost anybody and it took her two years to believe it.
recruits.greeting: Let me think for a moment. You will get a better answer and I will get less shouting.
recruits.home_note: In the Magic Quarter, surrounded by research.

background_sections.before:
A booth, a headset, and a career of being the invisible reason a room understood itself.

She is from Thessaloniki and had been in Brussels for eleven years. Her parents were at home. Greece and Belgium came down on different sides of a mountain range and she has worked out the implications more carefully than she has admitted to anyone.
background_sections.adjustment:
Two quiet years of being competent and assuming she was not.

What broke it was a goblin who asked her to interpret a contract dispute and then paid her properly and then came back.
background_sections.now:
Theramore, where four languages and two factions arrive on the same dock and nobody is being paid to make that work.

She makes it work, for money, and she has been in the room for three negotiations that would have gone badly without her.
background_sections.forward:
A grammar of this world's arcane. She is convinced the thing has a syntax and that every mage here is speaking it by ear.

Forty pages in. She has shown it to two people. One of them laughed and the other asked for a copy.

recruits.name: Ryan Murphy
recruits.backstory: Twelve years broking in Boston. Good at it, paid accordingly, and the deals he closed took things from people who never learned his name. He drank after work with men who did the same and agreed with them that it was the system, while not believing it even as he said it, and that's the only real difference between him and them. He expected the frontier to punish him. Instead it handed him a skill that's the same skill: read what a thing wants, work out what it'll take, close. Three years on he's more honest than he's ever been and no better a man, and he'll say so before you can.
recruits.greeting: Everything costs something. That's not a threat, it's the terms. I'll tell you the price before we start, which is more than my last employer ever did for me.
recruits.home_note: In the Magic Quarter, making deals by the summoning circle.

background_sections.before:
A desk, a screen, and a number that had to be bigger on Friday than it was on Monday.

He was raised in Cork by a grandmother who'd have had opinions. On balance he's glad she didn't live to form them.

He has a son, nineteen, who landed somewhere on this world and may well be looking. Ryan hasn't put his name on a single list at any hub in three years. He can give you the reasoning in one sentence and won't.
background_sections.adjustment: He hasn't had an adjustment. He's had a diagnosis, and he took it the way a man takes one he'd already privately made.
background_sections.now:
The Echo Isles, where nobody's under any illusion about anybody. He finds it restful.

His demons are on contracts he drafted and can recite clause by clause. He pays on time, exactly on time. That's not virtue, it's the only thing stopping the arrangement running the other direction.
background_sections.forward:
Out of the business. He's wanted out for fifteen years without once taking a step toward it, and he's fluent in the reasons.

What he does instead is keep the contracts clean and the terms honest and tell himself that's a different thing. Some days it is.

recruits.name: Carolina Santos
recruits.backstory: Twelve years a river pilot on the Amazon, which means twelve years of reading a water that redraws itself every season. A channel that was deep in March will ground you in September. She learned to feel the bottom through the hull. On this world the spirits of water hold a conversation with her that she describes as the same conversation, in an accent she had to work at.
recruits.greeting: Everything here has a current. Rivers, weather, people. Learn to feel it and you will stop fighting things that were already carrying you.

background_sections.before: A boat, a cargo, and a river two kilometres wide that her grandfather had read before her.
background_sections.adjustment:
Three gentle years, and she is clear-eyed about why: she arrived already believing the water was somebody.

Half the transplants she meets had to dismantle a whole worldview to get here. She walked in and recognised the place.
background_sections.now:
The Wetlands, where the water moves through the marsh in channels that shift with the rains and the local boatmen lose craft every spring.

She has been teaching two of them to read a bottom by feel. One of them is getting it, and watching that happen has done more for her than three years of being useful.
background_sections.forward:
She wants a river of her own on this world. A long one, with seasons, that she can learn for twenty years and still be surprised by.

She has been told there is one in Feralas. She has been told a great many things about Feralas.

recruits.name: Amber Whitehorse
recruits.backstory: Twenty-three years restoring wetland on the Oregon coast. It is a profession of doing something slow and correct and having nothing to show anybody for a decade. She planted sedge and waited. She pulled invasive grass for nine years in one basin. Druidry gave her the ability to make a thing grow in an afternoon, and the first year she used it constantly and the second year she mostly stopped.
recruits.greeting: Give it a season. Everything here gives you an answer if you let it finish.
recruits.home_note: Deep in the grove, defending the land.

background_sections.before:
Waders, a seed bank, and a grant cycle that funded three years of a thirty-year job.

She was divorced in 2016 and had made a reasonable peace with living alone. She says that peace is the single most useful thing she brought with her.
background_sections.adjustment:
Eight months, and she describes them as the easiest of her life, and she notices that this makes her poor company among transplants.

Her whole career had been patience without authority. Here she has both.
background_sections.now:
Feralas, in the wet country, where the growth is so fast that a mistake corrects itself in a season and a bad habit never gets caught.

She works the rot where the corruption has reached in. Slowly. The night elves have watched her for two years and she is aware that watching is how they decide.
background_sections.forward:
One basin, fully recovered, by her own hand, start to finish. She never got one on Earth. Three years in she is further along than twenty-three years of grant cycles took her.

She is also trying to work out how to teach restraint to people who can make a tree in an afternoon. So far she has one student and a lot of opinions.

recruits.name: Marcus Okafor
recruits.backstory: He spent a career being right early and watching it change nothing. Models, warnings, briefings to people whose job was deciding the warning was inconvenient. Here the storm answers him. He's been telling everyone he's fine about that since the day it started and everyone believes him, because he's also genuinely fine. Both are true. He's given up trying to reconcile them.
recruits.greeting: Pressure's dropping. No, listen. That's not thunder yet, that's the front arriving. We've got maybe four minutes and then it gets loud and I get useful.

background_sections.before:
Toronto. Instruments, a building, a window. He chased storms as a student, badly, in a Corolla, happily, then spent fifteen years watching them on screens from somewhere warm.

His mother in Lagos thought the job was a waste of a good degree and said so every Christmas until the last one.
background_sections.adjustment:
He treated the whole thing as fieldwork and it carried him through almost intact, which is better than most people managed and he knows it.

The part that wrecked him privately for a year: on Earth a storm was something he predicted and could never touch.
background_sections.now:
Durotar, where the dry storms come off the sea with no rain in them and the thunder arrives without warning.

His notes on where the strikes land have already told him something about this coast the orcs didn't know. He can't work out how to say so without sounding like every other outsider who ever turned up with a clipboard.
background_sections.forward:
A season's data written up, and one person on this world who cares what's in it. He's realistic about the odds and keeps the records anyway.

The thing he won't say out loud is that he'd like to stand in the middle of the biggest one there is. He's a meteorologist. He knows how that ends.

recruits.name: Ivan Petrov
recruits.backstory: Eleven years a tram driver in Novosibirsk. It is nobody's idea of a story and it is the whole reason he's good at this. Eleven years of a heavy thing on rails with other people's children stepping off kerbs. He never hit one. He maintains a two-handed weapon the same way: slow start, committed middle, and knowing exactly how long it takes to stop.
recruits.greeting: Stand where I can see you. If you're behind me I'll assume you're the enemy and I move faster than I apologise.
recruits.home_note: Deep in the chasm, where you found him.

background_sections.before: A cab, a route, and the same four stops in the dark every winter morning for eleven years.
background_sections.adjustment: He expected to be useless. He's a tram driver. What he found was that nobody here knows how to commit to a movement and then stop it, and that it's apparently a rare skill, and he's said out loud more than once that this world has very low standards.
background_sections.now:
Orgrimmar's Valley of Strength, where the traffic's worse than anything Novosibirsk managed and nobody's in charge of it.

He's begun directing it, unasked, at the worst hour. The orcs have started doing what he says.
background_sections.forward:
A route. He's asked three separate caravan masters whether anybody runs a fixed schedule and all three laughed.

He's going to keep asking. He thinks they're the ones being unreasonable and he may well be right.

recruits.name: Asher
recruits.backstory: Deep South, Bible Belt born and raised - you can hear it before he says three words. Says the fall into this world felt less like falling and more like being carried, though he laughs it off before it turns into a sermon. He's been camped outside the Coven for two days on his own, alone, waiting on nobody, because somebody's got to and he figures it might as well be him. Doesn't ask why you're here. Just asks if you could use the help, like it's the easiest question in the world.
recruits.greeting: Figure the Good Lord doesn't waste a resurrection on a man who's got nothing left to do with it. There's demons past that ridge. I mean to see to them. Walk with me, if you're willing.
recruits._design_note: Fixed/unchangeable companion - see world/recruit_manager.py RecruitNPC._build_asher_kit for his unique 2-ability kit and hand-authored gear, and /home/claude/frontier_rpg_docs/Asher_Coleman_Character_Profile.docx for the full handoff. Scripted to leave the party permanently after the Baneshadow quest turn-in (see world/quest_manager.py turn_in_quest). No home_town on purpose - he does not offer a find-me-later option at this stage.

background_sections.before:
Deep South, Bible Belt, and you can hear it inside three words. He will tell you about the place and not about himself, and he is so warm about it that you get most of the way home before you notice.

What anyone actually knows: he came through like everybody else, and he says the fall felt less like falling than like being carried. He laughs that off before it turns into a sermon. He always laughs it off.
background_sections.adjustment:
There is no record of Asher having an adjustment, and that is the strangest thing about him.

Everyone else can name their bad year. He was camped outside the Burning Blade Coven within days, alone, waiting for nobody in particular, on the grounds that somebody ought to be and it might as well be him. He asked no questions about where he was. He has still not asked any.
background_sections.now:
Wherever you are. He does not take contracts and he does not go home, and the one time somebody tried to send him back he was simply there the next morning, perfectly friendly about it.

He never asks why you are doing something. He asks if you could use the help, like it is the easiest question in the world, and it is very difficult to say no to.
background_sections.forward:
He has never stated a want. Not once, to anyone, in three years.

Asked, he turns it around and asks about yours, and he is so interested that it works every time. You will not notice he has done it until later, and then you will notice he has done it before.

recruits.name: Owen Pryce
recruits.backstory: Eight years a long-haul driver out of Cardiff, alone in a cab through the small hours, and the radio for company. He talked to himself for a living. Then he got here and something in the dark answered him, and the terrible part is that he was glad. He is aware of how that sounds. He says it anyway, early, so nobody can accuse him of hiding it later.
recruits.greeting: You hear that? No. Of course you do not. Stay close anyway.

background_sections.before:
Motorways, laybys, and a flat in Cardiff he barely lived in.

His mother was in a home in Barry and he visited every second Sunday for six years. She had forgotten who he was by the end. He says that makes this easier and the people who hear it understand that it does not.
background_sections.adjustment:
He fell straight in. There was no moment of resistance and he has examined that honestly and found it worse than the falling.

What he will say, when pressed: eight years of talking to nobody is good preparation for talking to something.
background_sections.now:
The Blasted Lands, where the air is thin with something and most people get headaches and leave.

He gets sentences. He stays.
background_sections.forward:
He wants to know what it wants. Properly. He has been given hints for three years and he is tired of hints.

He has also begun writing down what he hears, on the grounds that if he ever goes wrong, somebody will want a record of the route.

recruits.name: Mateo Rojas
recruits.backstory: Seventeen years of keeping the lights on at a mountaintop observatory above the Elqui valley. Technician, not astronomer, and he will correct you on that immediately and then talk for an hour anyway. Up there the sky is so clear it stops being scenery and becomes a place. He arrived on a world with the wrong stars in it and spent his first winter learning them from scratch, alone, on his back in the grass, happier than he had been in a decade.
recruits.greeting: Look up. Go on. Three years and I still have to make people look up.

background_sections.before:
Cold domes, cable runs, and the four hours before dawn when the astronomers slept and the mountain belonged to him.

He had a wife in La Serena and two girls who thought the mountain was boring. He agreed with them. He went anyway, every month, for seventeen years.
background_sections.adjustment:
He found the sky first and everything else second, in that order, and for a long while that worked.

The reckoning came in the second winter, when he had finished naming the constellations and had to go back down the mountain and be a person.
background_sections.now:
Tanaris, at the dark edge of the desert, where the air is dry and the nights go on forever.

The goblins think he is harmless and let him climb their towers. From the top of one of them he can see most of the sky at once, and he has begun to suspect it is the finest observing site on this world.
background_sections.forward:
A map of this sky, drawn properly, by somebody who understands that a sky is also a calendar and a clock and a promise. He is eleven months in.

He walks to the Tanaris hub twice a year with two names folded in his pocket, reads the whole list, and walks back. He talks about the stars on the way out and says very little on the way home.

recruits.name: Pasang Lama
recruits.backstory: Nineteen expeditions above eight thousand metres as a Solukhumbu climbing guide. He carried loads for people who went home famous. He has seen what high ground does to a body and to a personality, and he judges strangers by how they behave on day four. The spirits of stone and cold hold a conversation with him that he regards as a work arrangement rather than a mystery.
recruits.greeting: Slowly. The altitude here is nothing. Your pace is still wrong.

background_sections.before:
A load, a rope, and nineteen seasons of other people's ambition.

Four of his cousins did the same work. Two of them died on it. He has the names and he keeps them to himself.
background_sections.adjustment:
He said very little for the first year. He worked, ate, slept, and watched.

In the second year he began to speak and people discovered he had formed complete opinions about all of them.
background_sections.now:
Alterac's high valleys. Thin air, bad weather, and routes that were never written down.

He has written four of them down. He has shown them to one person.
background_sections.forward:
A summit nobody has stood on. He has heard there is one in Winterspring and he has heard a great deal of talk from people who have been halfway.

He would like to go alone. He is aware this is exactly what he spent nineteen years telling clients to stop wanting.

recruits.name: Haruto Nakamura
recruits.backstory: Thirty-one years of calligraphy in Kanazawa. The discipline is a single stroke, studied until the hand no longer requires the mind. He trained under a man who corrected him for eleven years before offering praise. Runework on this world responds to exactly that discipline and he was the only person who already had it, a circumstance he describes as luck and nobody who has watched him work believes.
recruits.greeting: The form matters. Not for ceremony. A rune cut carelessly fails carelessly, and it fails on whoever is standing closest.

background_sections.before:
Ink, paper, a master who died in 2017, and a studio with four students in it.

He never married. He has said that the work was a full occupation and he has said it in a tone that closes the subject.
background_sections.adjustment:
He asked to be taught. That was the whole of it, and it worked, and he is aware that almost no transplant tried it.

The tauren who agreed is dead now. Haruto finished the curriculum alone, from notes, and considers the result incomplete in ways he can specify.
background_sections.now:
Felwood, where the corruption has put something into the old rune-stones that nobody can read.

He is copying them before they finish degrading. It is slow, unrewarded, and the only record that will exist.
background_sections.forward:
Students. Four would be correct. He has two and is not inclined to lower the standard to reach four.

He is also assembling a reference of every rune form he has recorded, in the hope that the discipline outlasts the shortage of teachers. The hope is thin and he keeps working.

recruits.name: Liam Hartigan
recruits.backstory: Seventeen summers of bushfire season in New South Wales and the bad nights on the highway in between. Firefighter, then paramedic, then both, because the roster never cared which badge you held at three in the morning. The most useful thing in a burning room is a calm voice. The second most useful is a hand on the person about to run. He's good company. He hasn't slept properly since about 2019.
recruits.greeting: I've walked into worse than this. Stay behind me and breathe. No, actually breathe, out loud, where I can hear you doing it.

background_sections.before: A truck, a crew, and that particular silence in the cab on the way back from one that went badly.
background_sections.adjustment:
Easiest first year of his life, hardest second, and he can tell you the week it turned.

For twelve months the job was everywhere and nobody had to ask him. Then it went quiet for a season and he found out he has no idea what he's for without an emergency. There was no crew around to notice, which was most of the problem. The sun answers him the way a good crew does, when called and all at once, and he's given up pretending that isn't most of what holds him together.
background_sections.now:
Ashenvale East, working the ground around Grom's Rest where the corruption burns out of people slowly and nobody has a protocol for it.

He's written one. Four lines long, wrong in at least one place, and the only one that exists.
background_sections.forward:
A crew. Not companions. Rostered, trained, able to do it without him standing there.

It's the same thing he wanted on Earth and never got, and the reason he never got it was that he kept going in alone. Knowing that hasn't changed what he does when the call comes.

He's looked for nobody. There are two kids in Grom's Rest whose mother didn't come out of the corruption, and he's been in that village fourteen months, and everybody who knows him can see what's happened except him.

recruits.name: Marta Kowalski
recruits.backstory: Nineteen years of industrial sewing machines in a Łódź plant, which means nineteen years of being the only person in the building who could tell what was wrong from the sound. Management called her when a line stopped. They never once called her anything but by her first name. Goblin engineering is the same noise with more smoke, and she loves it in a way she'd be embarrassed to have written down.
recruits.greeting: Give it here. No, give it here. You've been hitting it, haven't you. People always hit it.

background_sections.before:
Forty machines, one toolkit, and a plant floor she could diagnose from the doorway.

Her husband worked the other shift for fifteen years so one of them was always home with the boys. The boys are grown. The husband was on his way to work.
background_sections.adjustment:
Three weeks, and she'd argue the three weeks were mostly about the language.

A machine's a machine. She was repairing goblin gear for money before she could ask where the toilet was.
background_sections.now:
Ratchet, where everything is broken and the goblins charge for the privilege.

She undercuts them by a third and fixes it properly. There's a goblin on the south pier who's threatened her twice and sent her work three times.
background_sections.forward:
Her own bench, her own sign, and nobody above her on a floor plan.

She's been quoted a price for a Ratchet pitch. She can afford it. She's found four reasons to wait and knows all four are the same reason.

recruits.name: Callum Reid
recruits.backstory: Sixteen years keeping reptiles at a Queensland sanctuary. Taipans, death adders, and the constant low-grade public relations work of explaining that the animal isn't malicious, it's frightened and you're enormous. He's been envenomated more often than any person should be and files all of it under professional development. His forearms are a map of the learning curve.
recruits.greeting: Don't worry about the scorpion. Mate, honestly. It's the least dangerous thing on me.

background_sections.before: A sanctuary, a hook, and school groups who all wanted to know the same thing about the same snake.
background_sections.adjustment:
Eighteen months of poisoning himself on purpose, alone, documented badly.

What he got out of it was a working relationship with things that kill people. Same relationship he had before. Better participants.
background_sections.now:
The Southern Barrens, within reach of the Wailing Caverns, where the serpents are a great deal more than serpents and hold firm views about intruders.

He goes in regularly and comes out reliably. The one time he brought something out alive the Crossroads made him promise not to do it again. He promised.
background_sections.forward:
He'd like to be bitten by whatever's at the bottom of the Caverns and survive it, and he knows exactly how that sentence reads.

His defensible position, and he will defend it: the thing that bites back is the thing that trusts you. He's yet to meet the animal that wasn't worth the conversation.

recruits.name: Emre Kaya
recruits.backstory: He started at nine, sent to fetch a stuck deadbolt for an uncle in the old bazaar, and found out that every lock is a short conversation with somebody who isn't in the room. Thirty doors a week for most of his life after that. He was never a thief. He was the man you called when you'd locked yourself out of your own livelihood, and he knew the inside of more businesses in that quarter than their owners did. Here the work's identical, except that once, with his picks still in the mechanism, the thing behind the door asked him a question. He got the door open. He's never said whether he answered.
recruits.greeting: A locked door is a conversation. Let me do the talking. You'll interrupt, everybody interrupts, and then it takes twice as long.

background_sections.before:
A roll of picks his uncle left him, and a quarter where four crafts died in his own lifetime while he watched.

*Bir kapı kapanır, bir kapı açılır.* One door closes, another opens. His mother said it constantly. He thought it was a proverb about God until he was about thirty and decided it was a proverb about him.
background_sections.adjustment:
None worth the name. A bigger bazaar with worse customers, and three contented years, which makes him odd company in any room of transplants.

The uncomfortable part, which he'll concede to somebody he likes: he's content partly because the shop is gone and so is everybody who'd have wanted it kept open a certain way. He didn't lose a family. He lost an obligation. He's been lighter since and he keeps that to himself.
background_sections.now:
Eastern Hillsbrad, in the country around Durnholde. A keep full of doors built by people who were serious about them.

He isn't looting it. He's reading it. Which lock came first, which were added after somebody got in, and therefore where somebody got in.
background_sections.forward:
The one that beats him. He hasn't met it and he's started to worry he never will, which is a strange thing to be frightened of, and he's frightened of it anyway.

Less romantically: an apprentice. The trade dies with him otherwise. He's watched that happen four times to men he knew.

recruits.name: Bakyt Asanov
recruits.backstory: Forty years of high pasture in the Tian Shan, moving a herd up in spring and down in autumn along a route his family has walked for six generations. He reads weather in a sky other people call clear and finds water where there is apparently none. The eagle he hunts with here is not the eagle he hunted with there, and he will tell you that the difference is less than you would think, and that he grieved the first one properly.
recruits.greeting: Walk behind me and step where I step. The ground lies. It lied at home too and I have forty years of practice.

background_sections.before:
A yurt, a herd, a route, and a father who taught him the route before he could ride.

Three sons, all of whom went to Bishkek for work. He understood why. It was still the end of six generations and both of those things sat in him at once for twenty years.
background_sections.adjustment:
He had the easiest first year of anyone and the quietest grief underneath it.

Nomads adjust. That is the whole profession. What he had to absorb was that this world has pasture his family will never walk, and he put a year of long evenings into getting comfortable with that.
background_sections.now:
The high country above Stonetalon, grass and wind and a long way between people.

The tauren there move herds on a cycle he recognised in about a week. They have begun asking his opinion on the cycle, which is the only honour he has ever visibly cared about.
background_sections.forward:
A route of his own. Mapped, seasonal, defensible, and walked often enough that somebody else could follow it after him.

He has two legs of it. He is fifty-eight and he has started to think about who gets it, and the thought has made him friendlier to strangers than he used to be.

recruits.name: Henrik Dahl
recruits.backstory: Twenty-one years a structural engineer in Copenhagen. The discipline is being certain that a thing will hold before anybody stands on it. Arcane magic rewards that temperament more than it rewards boldness, a fact he regards as the single most underappreciated feature of this world. He is precise in conversation to a degree people find either restful or maddening, and he has never managed to predict which.
recruits.greeting: Before we begin: what is the actual objective? I have found that parties rarely agree, and discover it halfway through.

background_sections.before:
Load calculations, tolerances, and a career of being the person who said no to architects.

His wife taught at the university. She had a nine o'clock lecture and the Integration arrived at ten past. He has worked out, with some care, that she would therefore have been in a lecture theatre, and he has stopped the calculation precisely there, every time, for three years.
background_sections.adjustment:
Twenty months, documented. He treated himself as a structure under an unfamiliar load and tested accordingly.

The resulting notes are the most useful document on arcane tolerance anyone has produced here, and he regards them as preliminary, and he will argue the point.
background_sections.now:
Dalaran's outskirts, as close to the shattered workings as the wards permit, where the arcane behaves in ways that would be unreproducible anywhere else.

He measures. He has filled eleven books and will tell you the eleventh is the only one worth reading.
background_sections.forward:
A standard. Not a spell and not a discovery: a published figure that other casters can work to, so that the next person who tries this does not have to find the limit with their own body.

He has calculated his own limits to four significant figures and he does not approach them, which is the whole of his method and the reason he is still alive.

recruits.name: Anjali Nair
recruits.backstory: Thirty-one years teaching botany in Pune. Three decades of patience with slow things, and with students who wanted results by Friday. A plant will tell you what it needs if you are willing to wait several seasons for the sentence to finish. Druidry asked her for the same patience and gave her, for the first time in her life, the ability to answer back.
recruits.greeting: Gently. Gently, now. Whatever is wrong here, shouting at it will make it worse. I have thirty years of evidence.

background_sections.before:
A department, a herbarium, and four decades of pressed specimens she labelled in her own hand.

Her husband retired in 2018 and spent two years teaching himself to cook. She had one year of that. She describes the year as the best of her marriage and she says it in a voice that invites no follow-up.
background_sections.adjustment:
Slowly, which suited her. She treated the whole first year as a field season and kept a notebook in the way she had kept forty of them.

The notebook is now the only systematic record of Ashenvale's understory that exists in any language, and she regards it as a draft.
background_sections.now:
Ashenvale, where the forest is sick in a patterned way and the night elves know it in their bones without having ever written it down.

She is writing it down. The Sentinels were suspicious for two years and now bring her specimens.
background_sections.forward:
She would like to be read in two hundred years. She says this cheerfully and she is entirely serious.

Which means a copy somewhere safe, in a language that will survive, and a student who cares. She has the first. She is working on the third.

recruits.name: Hana Tamihana
recruits.backstory: Fourteen summers of black sand and heavy water on the Waikato coast, and a rip that took somebody every few years no matter how many signs went up. She's pulled a lot of people out. She remembers the two she didn't, by name, including the one whose family still sends her nothing. She was nineteen when she got here, into a world of people with whole careers behind them, and spent a year being treated as the kid. That's the part that actually stung.
recruits.greeting: Stay on my left and don't argue with it. Water's not your mate and it's not your enemy. It's honest. People drown because they try to negotiate.

background_sections.before:
The beach. Patrol, flags, and a tower her uncle sat in before her.

The water taught her the only thing about water that matters and she's never needed a second lesson.
background_sections.adjustment:
Less to unlearn than most, and she'll tell you flat that's luck and not merit.

The tide spirits read her the way she reads a break. Take what's offered, give back, never turn your back on it. The whole arrangement was legible inside a week. Her real adjustment was social and it took three years.
background_sections.now:
The Hillsbrad coast. Colder and greyer than home, same undertow.

She's been teaching the fishing families to read it. Two of them listen. One of those two has stopped losing nets, and that's done more for her standing in Southpoint than anything she could have said about herself.
background_sections.forward:
A bigger sea. She says it lightly and she means it: there's a coast west of Ashenvale where the water apparently does something nobody can describe properly to her, and that's her problem now.

She's also working west because west is where the transit hub is, and the hub is where the lists go up. She checks them. Her whole family was at the beach that morning, so they're somewhere, and nineteen-year-olds don't accept somewhere the way older people have learned to.

recruits.name: Kesten Ambrose
recruits.backstory: Tallinn, the city archive, twenty-six years among acid-free boxes. Then a serial number in a Scourge ledger. Then neither. What came back has the archivist's habits and little of his warmth, and he is the first to say so. He catalogues. It is the only continuity he has and he defends it the way other people defend a family.
recruits.greeting: Kesten. Formerly a serial number. I have selected the name and I would ask you to use it.

background_sections.before:
Stacks, acid-free boxes, and the quiet conviction that a thing unrecorded has not quite happened.

There was a wife. He has her name written down because he no longer trusts himself to hold it, and he regards the written record as sufficient, and nobody who hears him say so finds it sufficient at all.
background_sections.adjustment:
The question does not apply in the usual form. He did not adjust to this world. He returned to it, partially, and has been taking inventory of what came back ever since.

The inventory is the document he values most and he will not show it to anyone.
background_sections.now:
Tirisfal, close to the ground he was processed on, where the ledgers are still legible if you know the hand.

He knows the hand. He has been reading his own entry for two years and has never told anyone what it says.
background_sections.forward:
A complete record of the Scourge's working, written by something that was inside it. He is aware of what he is for. He has decided to be for that deliberately rather than by default.

He expects to finish nothing. The expectation has never once slowed him.

recruits.name: Tarek Mansour
recruits.backstory: Fourteen years a civil engineer in Cairo. Water systems: pressure, pumps, the unglamorous arithmetic of a city that drinks. He was good at it and he was careful about everything else, for a long time, until a colleague made a telephone call about him and the wrong office took an interest. He left in a week with two bags and an engineering degree nobody in Berlin would look at. The faith he carries now is not the one that was used against him, and he will sit with you for an hour explaining the difference to anyone prepared to be serious about it.
recruits.greeting: Tell me plainly where I am needed. I have had my fill of the other kind of instruction, from people who were very sure they were doing right.

background_sections.before:
Pipes, pumps, pressure, and a flat in Heliopolis he could still draw from memory if he let himself.

There was a man. Omar, who taught secondary-school chemistry and laughed at everything, including this. They were careful for six years and careless once, at a wedding, in front of someone who counted it.

Omar stayed. He had parents and a sister and no money, and he told Tarek to go and meant it. That is the last conversation they had.
background_sections.adjustment:
He is the rare case for whom this world was an improvement, he says so plainly, and it silences rooms.

Two reasons, and he gives them in order. The first is that the thing poisoning the water here is a visible enemy that can be fought, and he waited twenty years for an enemy that simple. The second he gives more quietly: in three years on this world, nobody has asked him a question he had to lie about.
background_sections.now:
Ashenvale East, working the streams that come down out of the corrupted country, where the water carries the rot further than the rot can walk.

He has mapped which springs are still clean and which only look it, and the Splintertree garrison now sends for him before it sends for a priest.

The orcs have offered him a title twice. He has declined twice, politely, and given no reason either time. The reason is that he has watched what happens to a man who gets to decide who belongs.
background_sections.forward:
A well that is still standing in ten years. He has sunk three. One has already failed, and he can tell you precisely why, at length, with a stick in the dirt.

He has stopped describing this as rebuilding. He calls it building. That distinction took him two years to arrive at and he holds it firmly.

He walks down to the Astranaar hub every few months and reads the Cairo lists. Omar is not on them. That means very little and he knows exactly how little it means, which is the problem with being a man who understands probability.

recruits.look: Egyptian man in his late 30s, medium height and thickening at the middle, close-cropped black hair receding at the temples, heavy brows, a careful unhurried face. Dark leather tank harness over a padded gambeson in sand and oxblood, a broad round shield, a short heavy blade kept sheathed. A pair of white cotton conservator's gloves folded through his belt, laundered grey.

recruits.name: Fiona Strachan
recruits.backstory: Nine years in fraud investigation in Dublin. The whole trade is noticing the one entry that doesn't fit and then being unbearable about it until somebody checks. She was very unpopular and quite often right. The thing that hunts people here leaves a trail of the same shape as a cooked ledger: too neat, and neat in the places nobody looks.
recruits.greeting: I've read your file. Not yours, obviously. I'm saying that's the habit and you'll want to know about it before we work together.

background_sections.before: Spreadsheets, interviews, and a reputation among colleagues that she earned and never enjoyed.
background_sections.adjustment:
Her first year was a filing exercise. She catalogued every corrupted thing she met and the notebook is now more use than she is.

Somewhere in the second year she worked out she'd been treating a war as a casework backlog. That one landed hard.
background_sections.now:
Western Plaguelands. The corruption's patterned here and nobody's mapped the pattern.

She's mapping it. Three hundred pages, cross-referenced, and she carries the whole thing on her back because she won't leave a copy anywhere she can't see.
background_sections.forward:
Finish the catalogue. Hand it to somebody who'll act on it. Both halves matter and the second is the one she keeps failing at.

She's had the same conversation with the Argent Dawn four times. She takes minutes of those too.

recruits.look: Scottish woman in her mid 40s, tall and square-built, sandy-grey hair cut short and shoved back, weather-ruined face, pale eyes set deep. Blackened mail over a long coat in slate and rust, a heavy tower shield slung at her back, a flanged mace at her hip. A yellow offshore survival-suit whistle still clipped to her collar on a fraying lanyard.

recruits.name: Pavlo Hryn
recruits.backstory: Sixteen years a Lviv schoolteacher, history, fourteen-year-olds. The work is standing in front of a room that would rather be anywhere else and keeping it together by presence alone. He does the same thing in a shield wall and finds it considerably easier, because a gnoll at least wants something comprehensible.
recruits.greeting: Give me the line and I'll hold it. Tell me how long. I'd rather know.

background_sections.before:
A classroom, a curriculum he disagreed with, and thirty children a year he mostly managed to reach.

He taught the same four wars every spring. He's noticed nobody here needs a history teacher and it's taken most of three years to stop being wounded by that.
background_sections.adjustment:
Badly, and he's open about it. For a year he looked for a school.

There isn't one. There's a lot of work for a man who'll stand still while something comes at him, and he took it, and the taking was a small grief he's never dressed up as a calling.
background_sections.now:
Southshore, holding the line against whatever walks down from the Plaguelands.

It's steady work and he's good at it and he'd swap it tomorrow.
background_sections.forward:
He's still going to teach. Six children in Southshore, twice a week, whatever he can remember of a world that isn't coming back.

Two of them have stopped attending. He's decided not to ask why.

recruits.look: Ukrainian man in his early 50s, huge through the shoulders and gone soft over it, shaved head, grey stubble, a nose broken long ago and badly set. Dark iron plate with a black tabard and a greatshield, faint ember-red light in the seams of the gauntlets. A steel thermos flask, dented and lidless, strapped where a water flask should go.

recruits.name: Jun-seo Park
recruits.backstory: Nine years on a Busan line, night shift mostly, the same two motions ten thousand times a day. His body learned things his mind never had a say in. Here that's a weapon: he moves without deciding to and it's fast, and the only thing that frightens him about it is how little of it he chooses.
recruits.greeting: Twelve hours a day for nine years, standing up, in the same two square metres. Whatever this is, it's easier.

background_sections.before:
A line, a shift bell, and two square metres of floor he could draw from memory.

He sent money home every month for nine years. His parents are in Busan or they're not. The hub for that city came down in the far north, past the ice, and the arithmetic of that is not something he's prepared to do out loud.
background_sections.adjustment:
The first year he worked. Anything, for anyone, as many hours as there were.

The second year somebody made him sit down and he found out he had no idea what to do with a day. He'd be the first to say that's a worse problem than the first year's.
background_sections.now:
Thousand Needles, the high mesas, where the only way up is a lift and the lift takes its time.

He runs the baskets. It's two motions, ten thousand times. He's aware of the joke and he keeps the job anyway.
background_sections.forward:
He wants to be slow at something. Not good. Slow. He's picked woodcarving because it can't be hurried and he's catastrophically bad at it.

That's the point. He's explained this twice and neither person understood.

recruits.look: South Korean man in his early 40s, wiry and slightly stooped, black hair shot with grey and flattened by a helmet, a long patient face, deep smile lines he does not use often. Grey-black mail with a hooded mantle and a scythe-headed polearm carried butt-down. A welder's flip-up shade, cracked across one lens, pushed up on his forehead.

recruits.name: Minh Tran
recruits.backstory: Twenty-three years of air traffic control at Tân Sơn Nhất. The profession is holding forty futures in your head simultaneously and choosing the one in which nobody dies. Time magic asked him for exactly that and nothing he had not already done for two decades on three hours of sleep. He is the calmest person in most rooms and it is entirely professional conditioning rather than temperament.
recruits.greeting: A moment. I would like to establish the sequence of events before we add to it.

background_sections.before:
A dark room, a scope, and the discipline of never once letting your voice carry what your pulse is doing.

He has a daughter who was studying in Melbourne. Two hubs, two continents, and a survivable set of assumptions. He has permitted himself the survivable set.
background_sections.adjustment: He was on shift, and he has said that the handover was the hardest part, and the people who hear that assume he means the Integration. He means the handover.
background_sections.now:
The Caverns of Time approach, where the sequence of events is negotiable and almost nobody understands how dangerous that is.

He has appointed himself to the approach. No one asked him to. He has made a rota of one.
background_sections.forward:
He would like one hour in which nothing is his responsibility. He has not had one since 2003 and he is beginning to suspect the problem is not the schedule.

In the meantime he keeps the gate, because nobody else will, which is precisely the reasoning that got him here.

recruits.look: Vietnamese man in his late 30s, slight and neat, black hair parted and kept flat, round wire glasses, an attentive head-tilted way of standing. Pale blue and bone-white robes with long cuffs and a brass-ringed orrery at the belt, a slim staff with a slow-turning ring at its head. A tuning fork on a cord round his neck, the tines worn bright.

recruits.name: Alonso Vega
recruits.backstory: Twenty-two years running a kiln in Talavera de la Reina. Glaze, temperature, timing: a trade where the whole year's work turns on four hours of heat going exactly right. He feels a fire the way other people feel a draught. On this world fire answers him and the first thing he did with that was make a cup, badly, and he keeps it on a shelf.
recruits.greeting: Give me room. More than that. Honestly, more than that, I have burnt three people's eyebrows off being polite about it.

background_sections.before: A kiln, a wheel, and a workshop his grandfather fired for forty years before him.
background_sections.adjustment:
Ten weeks. He treated it as a new kiln with an unfamiliar character and learned it the way he had learned four others.

His wife in Talavera was at the market when it happened. He has said the word market perhaps twice in three years and each time changed the subject so quickly that whoever he was talking to apologised.
background_sections.now:
The Searing Gorge. It is the hottest place anybody has told him about, so it is the only place he wants to be.

The Thorium Brotherhood use him and underpay him. He has a pot going in a crack in the rock face that nobody is supposed to know about.
background_sections.forward:
A kiln. His own, built right, with somebody to teach.

He has the clay. He has the site. He has been putting it off for two years and the reason he gives is money, and the reason is not money.

recruits.look: Mexican man in his mid 40s, broad and short, thick black hair pushed back off a high forehead, forearms shiny with old burn scars, a wide easy face. Deep orange and ash-grey robes cut short at the sleeve for the heat, a censer-headed staff trailing warm light. A pair of smoked-glass glassblower's goggles hung at his throat.

recruits.name: Delroy Beckford
recruits.backstory: Thirty-one years of nights in a bakery on Spanish Town Road. In at eleven, out at seven, measuring by hand and by feel. He knew the weather by how the dough behaved and the regulars by what they bought. A brew is a dough with different patience. He treats a wounded party like an order going out at dawn: everybody gets something, nobody waits long, and the complaining is part of the process.
recruits.greeting: Sit. Drink that. No, I'm not telling you what's in it, you wouldn't thank me. Thirty-one years I fed a city its breakfast and not one of them asked what was in the bread either.

background_sections.before: The night shift. He's never in his life been awake at the same hours as everybody else, and he's never once called that a sacrifice.
background_sections.adjustment: Four in the morning his time. That's the only reason he wasn't asleep when it happened, and he says so like a joke. It's not entirely a joke and he knows which parts are which.
background_sections.now:
Booty Bay, lower gallery. The pier work breaks people steadily and the Baron doesn't care.

He works nights out of habit. The bruisers have a following among themselves that pretends not to be a queue.

Every ship that ties up gets the same three names asked of it. The Bay thinks that's a charming habit of the old baker's. It's a system, it's why he took a pitch on the gallery instead of up the hill, and in three years it's produced one maybe.
background_sections.forward:
An oven. Then an apprentice. In that order, and he won't be hurried on either.

Twice he's been offered a share in a Bay kitchen. Twice he's said no, for reasons he gives freely and nobody finds convincing.

recruits.look: Jamaican man in his early 50s, tall and lean with a slight permanent stoop, grey locs tied back, a long lined face that goes from grave to delighted with no warning. Leather and woven-grass healer's gear in moss and bone, a cauldron-bowl slung at the hip and a short paddle-like stave. A floury canvas apron, folded and tied at the waist, never quite clean.

recruits.name: Imelda Salonga
recruits.backstory: Fish on a Navotas quay from five in the morning, boxing in the evenings, the same six streets her whole life. Ten fights a year and she won more than she lost. Her healing isn't gentle and doesn't look like healing. She hits things and her people get better. The Vine Road took about a week to stop asking and the better part of a year to stop watching her sideways while it worked.
recruits.greeting: I know how it looks. Stay behind me and watch. When I land one you'll feel it. I could never explain this in my own language either, so.

background_sections.before:
A stall, a gym above a tyre shop, and hands she wrapped herself because nobody else did it tight enough.

Her mother called the boxing a phase for nineteen years, then turned up at Freewind Post two summers ago on a goblin barge, having asked after her in four languages the whole way down the coast. She lives in the Post now. She still calls it a phase.
background_sections.adjustment: She landed at market hour with her hands already wrapped. She calls that luck and nobody's talked her out of it.
background_sections.now:
Freewind Post, where the tauren walk the lifts and the drop does the rest. The injured come in steadily all week.

The Post asks for her by name without being able to say what she is. She still wraps her hands before anything else, breakfast included.
background_sections.forward:
She's been asking around the arena whether anybody here fights properly. Rules. A count. Somebody keeping time.

The answers have all been enthusiastic and none of them have been about that, and she's getting tired of explaining the difference.

recruits.look: Filipina woman in her mid 30s, compact and visibly strong through the shoulders, black hair in a short practical knot, flat nose, a scar through one eyebrow. Mail and green hide cut for movement, wrapped fists, no shield and no staff at all. A pair of soft hand-wraps from a boxing gym, washed to grey, rewound every morning.

recruits.name: Tomas Havel
recruits.backstory: Eighteen years up in the grid in Prague, on tour and in houses, at four in the morning, hanging weight over the heads of people who'd never once look up. The job was leverage, timing, and never being the reason something fell. He swings a two-hander like a man who's spent his life moving heavy things through small gaps. He still hasn't drawn it on anything worse than a training post and he's in no rush to change that.
recruits.greeting: Big sword, lots of room. Tell me where you want me standing before it starts, not during. I've worked with people who shout during. I didn't enjoy any of them.

background_sections.before: A bad shoulder from a truss in 2014 that he worked through because the show was that night. It still tells him when the weather's turning and he still works through it.
background_sections.adjustment: He arrived forty feet up, which should have killed him, and he's never once managed to tell that story without it coming out as a brag. He's given up fixing the delivery and now just gets it over with early.
background_sections.now:
Fenris Isle and whatever scaffolding he can reach, because people here build fast and tie off badly and he physically can't walk past it.

He's paid in food and the occasional argument.
background_sections.forward:
Something that stays up.

He has been looking at the way this city holds its roofs on with an expression the orcs find difficult to read and have decided not to ask about.

There was a woman in Prague he hadn't asked yet, and before her a lighting tech called Dominik who asked him first and had a yes inside the week. The crew ran a book on which way he'd go. He refused to settle it for them, mostly because he liked watching the money change hands.

Three years is long enough that he has started describing both of them in the past tense without noticing. His friends here have noticed.

recruits.look: Czech man in his early 40s, rangy and long-armed, dark hair cut short, a thin face with a permanent squint from years of looking up into lights. Battered plate with the pauldrons stripped off for reach, a two-handed sword worn across the back. A steel carabiner clipped to his belt loop, scratched to bare metal.

recruits.name: Eino Virtanen
recruits.backstory: Twenty-six years felling timber in Lapland. Six months of dark a year, machinery, and nobody to talk to for days at a stretch. The axe is the same axe. The cold's the same cold. He talks about as much as the work required. People read that as unfriendliness for the first month and then stop.
recruits.greeting: Cold doesn't bother me. Go on. Say something about the sauna. Everybody does and I've stopped minding.

background_sections.before: Timber, a machine, and a stretch of forest the size of a county.
background_sections.adjustment: Nothing to speak of. The trees here are bigger.
background_sections.now:
Winterspring. Snow, dark, and timber the size of towers.

The Everlook crews hire him by the season and have given up trying to make conversation. He prefers the arrangement and thinks they do too.
background_sections.forward:
He'd like to see the north of this world. Not for any reason he can give. He's been told Northrend's worse than Lapland and that's done nothing to put him off.

His brother worked the same ground and they haven't spoken since before. Eino's mentioned this twice in three years, both times in passing, both times to nobody in particular.

recruits.look: Finnish man in his late 30s, enormous and pale, red-blond hair and a thick beard, small light eyes, a face that gives away nothing. Heavy hide and fur over bare arms, a hand axe in each fist. A length of orange pipeline marking tape knotted round one bicep, faded to salmon.

recruits.name: Ziad Haddad
recruits.backstory: Six years a paramedic in Beirut, a city that taught him triage as a reflex and the bitter arithmetic of a van with four spaces. He made those choices for six years and every one of them was correct and every one of them cost him something. Fel magic put a terrible, obvious power in reach and he took it, and his reasoning is the same reasoning that let him choose the fourth patient.
recruits.greeting: Keep moving. I am serious. Everything bad that happened to me happened while I was standing still.

background_sections.before: A van, a radio, and a city where the road you took mattered more than the medicine you carried.
background_sections.adjustment:
Twelve months of saying yes to things he should have slept on.

He will own all of it. What he refuses is the suggestion that it was weakness. He was offered the ability to save more people and he took it, and three years on he is still doing the arithmetic in public, out loud, for anyone who wants to argue.
background_sections.now:
Desolace, around the Scar, where the gnolls and the satyr trade the ground back and forth and the casualties are constant.

He is first on scene. Always. The centaur have a word for him and he has asked three times what it means and been told three different things.
background_sections.forward:
Out. He wants out of it, and he has looked into what that costs, and the figure is the reason he is still in.

In the meantime he works. The people he pulls out of the Scar are alive either way, and that is the whole of his defence and he knows how thin it is.

recruits.look: Lebanese man in his early 30s, slim and quick, black curls kept long on top, a sharp handsome face he is aware of, dark eyes with a faint green cast now. Purple-black leathers cut close with a half-cape, twin curved blades, a thin fel shimmer on the edges. A single foam earplug on a cord, tucked behind his collar.

recruits.name: Pieter Malan
recruits.backstory: Twenty-eight years in Rotterdam port safety. Harnesses, exclusion zones, and the deeply unglamorous business of nobody dying today. He's been shouted at by thousands of men in a hurry and outlasted all of them. He stands in front of a party now and runs the same arithmetic he always has. A precaution costs less than the thing it prevents, every time, on any world.
recruits.greeting: I'll take the hits. That's not courage, it's arithmetic: I'm the one wearing the armour.

background_sections.before: A clipboard, a hard hat, and a reputation as the most tedious man on the dock.
background_sections.adjustment: Instant, and he's slightly ashamed of how instant. His entire profession turned out to be directly applicable to a world with monsters in it, and his colleagues on Earth would have found that hilarious.
background_sections.now:
Booty Bay, the piers, where men work above water with no harness and the Baron's position on this is that they chose the job.

Pieter has pulled nine men out in three years. He keeps the number because somebody should.
background_sections.forward:
Rules that outlive him. He's written a set for the Bay's pier work and the Baron has ignored all of them.

He submits them again every season. Four seasons now.

recruits.look: South African man in his mid 40s, heavy and sunburnt, thinning blond hair, a flat pugnacious face, forearms like a man who has swung things for a living. Dull gold plate worn open at the throat, a one-handed mace and a shield he uses offensively. A groundsman's folding knife on a belt loop, handle worn pale.

recruits.name: Esteban Ruiz
recruits.backstory: Nineteen years a Valparaíso surgeon. The trade consists of doing a violent thing for a good reason, with absolute precision, while the person on the table trusts you entirely. Blood magic is the identical proposition with the formalities removed. He finds the honesty of it a relief and the company it attracts a continual disappointment.
recruits.greeting: There is a price. I will name it before we proceed, and I would ask you not to pretend afterwards that I did not.

background_sections.before: Theatre lists, a scalpel, and twenty years of consent forms he insisted on explaining properly even when nobody wanted him to.
background_sections.adjustment:
He had no crisis. He had an inventory, and he conducted it in the first month, and found the skill transferred entire.

What he underestimated was how much of his old restraint had been supplied by the hospital rather than by him. He discovered this in year two and did not enjoy the discovery.
background_sections.now:
Stranglethorn's interior, where the Bloodsail will pay anything for a man who can keep the injured alive and who does not ask about the injuries.

He asks. Every time, on the record, and then treats them anyway.
background_sections.forward:
A standard of practice, written down, binding on anyone who claims the discipline. There is nothing of the kind on this world and the absence appals him.

He has drafted eleven clauses. He expects no one to adopt them and continues to draft.

recruits.look: Argentinian man in his late 30s, medium build and going grey early at the front, neat beard, an unsettlingly calm bedside manner. Dark red leathers with a lamellar chest and a thin crimson blade, faint red light under the skin of his forearms. A radiation-badge dosimeter clipped at his collar, the window long since gone black.

recruits.name: Kiet Somsak
recruits.backstory: Eleven years a Bangkok motorcycle courier, which means eleven years of being invisible in traffic and arriving before anyone expected. He went into offices, kitchens, and back rooms all day long and nobody ever looked at him twice. He kept a great deal of what he overheard. Here the skill transfers whole and he has been careful to let very few people work out that it is a skill.
recruits.greeting: Keep your voice down. Half of what I know, I learned from people who thought nobody was listening.

background_sections.before:
A bike, a bag, and a city where the fastest route changed hourly.

He lived with his grandmother in Khlong Toei. She was eighty-four and she could not manage the stairs.
background_sections.adjustment:
Six weeks. He had a route in Orgrimmar before he had a bed.

He says the hard part was the quiet. Eleven years of engine noise and then a world where he can hear people breathing two rooms away.
background_sections.now:
Orgrimmar, the Drag, where everybody talks and nobody watches the person carrying something.

He carries something. He has mapped the whole city by how long each route takes at each hour, which is the first thing he does anywhere, and he has stopped being surprised that nobody else does it.
background_sections.forward:
A standing arrangement with somebody who pays for information and asks for it politely. He has had three offers and all three were from people he would rather owe nothing to.

He would also like to stop flinching at silence. Three years in, it is slower going than the rest of it.

recruits.look: Thai man in his late 20s, small and economical in his movements, black hair cut short, a quiet watchful face, hands that are never still. Matte grey-green leathers with a soft hood down, a thin dagger at the small of the back. A brass key blank on a loop of wire at his belt, cut for nothing.

recruits.name: Stelios Dukas
recruits.backstory: Nineteen years a Thessaloniki funeral director. The trade is composure, paperwork, and being the steadiest person in the worst room of somebody's life. He is unshockable in a way that has nothing to do with callousness, and his profession prepared him for this world considerably better than anybody's did who arrived with a weapon.
recruits.greeting: I handled the dead for nineteen years before any of this. The difference now is that they occasionally have something to add.

background_sections.before:
Arrangements, families, and the particular courtesy of a man who has told four thousand people the worst thing they will hear that year.

The business was his father's. He has said that inheriting it was not a choice and that he would have chosen it, and that both of those are true, and that people find the combination difficult.
background_sections.adjustment: He was calm throughout and he is tired of being praised for it. Composure was his occupation for nineteen years. Praising him for it is like praising a baker for being awake.
background_sections.now:
The Undercity, where the dead are a civil service and somebody with his background is either a gift or an affront depending on who is asking.

He does the paperwork. He is extremely good at the paperwork, and he has used it four times now to find out who a body was before it stopped being anyone.
background_sections.forward:
Rites. Proper ones, for the transplants who die here with nobody who knows their language.

He has conducted one hundred and forty. He keeps a register, and he has written to every hub he can reach asking that the names be posted, and three have replied.

recruits.look: Greek man in his early 50s, tall and gaunt, grey hair worn too long, a dry ironic face, half-moon reading glasses on a chain. Charcoal and bone robes with a high collar, a staff topped with a bound sheaf of pages. A librarian's date stamp, brass and wooden-handled, carried in a robe pocket.

recruits.name: Ratih Pranoto
recruits.backstory: Fifteen years a Sumatran forest ranger, which meant long patrols, poachers, and a government that funded the uniforms and little else. She learned to read a forest for the one wrong thing in it: a snare, a path, a silence where there should be birds. Here the forests are stranger and the method is identical, and she has found the one wrong thing four times in three years.
recruits.greeting: Walk quieter. I can hear you from the other end of the valley and so can everything else.

background_sections.before:
A patrol route, a rifle she rarely carried, and the particular loneliness of being the only person in the province who cared.

She has a sister in Medan and a nephew she had promised to visit.
background_sections.adjustment:
She went to work. Within a month she had a patrol route of her own invention and nobody's permission.

The second year was harder, and it was harder for a reason she finds absurd: out here people thank her.
background_sections.now:
Northern Ashenvale, walking a route she drew herself, looking for the one wrong thing.

She has reported every find to the Sentinels and signed none of the reports.
background_sections.forward:
She wants the Sentinels to take her on properly. Rostered, briefed, part of a line instead of a woman in the woods.

She has asked twice. The answers were polite. She is going to ask a third time and she has decided what she will say if the answer is the same.

recruits.look: Indonesian woman in her late 30s, slim and weathered, black hair in a tight braid, a direct unsmiling face, fine squint lines. Green and grey leathers with a quiver worn high, a long recurve bow. A brass river-gauge plate, stamped with marks, sewn flat onto her sleeve.

recruits.name: Kourosh Behzadi
recruits.backstory: Twelve years pricing mortality for a Tehran insurer. The work of establishing, very carefully, how likely a thing is. He finds arcane magic restful by comparison because for once the numbers hold still. He's the only person on this side of the mountains who's calculated his own odds and he won't tell anybody the figure. The refusal is cheerful rather than grim. People find that worse.
recruits.greeting: I'm going to stand back here and be extremely precise. You're welcome to be brave. Somebody in a group should be and it was never going to be the actuary.

background_sections.before:
Tables, reserving, a good office with a bad view, and a mother he telephoned on Fridays who thought the job was beneath him.

She was right that he was capable of more. She was wrong about what more would have meant.

He priced her odds in the second year, properly, using what's known about hub placement and survivorship, and then he stopped looking, because an actuary who won't act on his own table isn't an actuary. He's never told anybody the figure. He's never told anybody there was one.
background_sections.adjustment: He arrived mid-calculation and the first thing he did on this world was finish the sum. That was momentum, not bravery, and he's irritated that people keep wanting it to be the other thing.
background_sections.now:
The Crystalline Underdark, where the lattice does something to arcane magic that nobody has characterised.

He's characterising it. The case is nearly full.
background_sections.forward:
No press, no journal, no readership, and he's writing it anyway. Longhand, in a case he keeps dry.

He's told two people what's in it. Both changed the subject. He recorded the date each time.

recruits.look: Iranian man in his late 30s, slender and slightly formal in his bearing, black hair neatly cut, close beard, a face that looks faintly amused at all times. Indigo and silver robes with precise geometric trim, a staff of nested rotating rings. A slim mechanical pencil, silver, clipped inside the collar of his robe.

recruits.name: Driss Alaoui
recruits.backstory: Twenty-eight years guiding caravans out of Zagora, across ground where a wrong turn costs a camel and a second wrong turn costs a man. He reads sand the way a sailor reads water. The desert spirits here required an introduction and then settled into something he finds entirely familiar: a long relationship with a landscape that would kill him on a technicality.
recruits.greeting: Water first. Then we talk about whatever you came here to say.

background_sections.before:
Camels, tourists, and a route his father and his father's father had walked.

He raised four children on it. Three are grown. The fourth was nine.
background_sections.adjustment:
He asked the land for permission in his own language and something answered. He mentions this rarely.

The rest of the adjustment was practical: new stars, new seasons, and a year of getting the distances right.
background_sections.now:
Tanaris, out of Gadgetzan, where the goblins pay for a man who gets cargo across intact.

He gets it across. He has refused two contracts over the water allowance and both parties came back with a better one.
background_sections.forward:
A route across Tanaris that a caravan can use in summer. There is a way through and he has most of it.

Finishing it means four more seasons of walking and he has the seasons.

recruits.look: Moroccan man in his mid 40s, lean and long-limbed, black hair greying at the temples under a wrapped headscarf, a narrow thoughtful face. Blue-grey mail and layered cloth with a totem stave and a horn at his belt, static lifting the loose ends of the scarf. A torque wrench, short and stubby, slung in a loop at his hip.

recruits.name: Marisol Quintero
