recruits.backstory: Nine years in a Bogotá emergency department, three of them on nights, all of them short-staffed. She learned to keep a frightened person talking while her hands did something they would rather not watch. The Light moves through her easily and she treats it as one more instrument on a tray. The habit of narrating came with her and half the party finds it steadying and half find it maddening.
recruits.greeting: Talk to me while I work. Anything. I do better with a voice in the room and so do you.

background_sections.before:
Trolleys in a corridor, a triage board, and a city that produced a steady supply.

Her brother was a motorcycle courier in the same city. She patched him up twice. The second time she shouted at him in the corridor for ten minutes and she would give anything to have that back.
background_sections.adjustment:
Eighteen months of working flat out, and she will tell you honestly that she did it to stay out of her own head.

It worked. She would do it again. She is also aware of what it is.
background_sections.now:
Dustwallow, out of Theramore, working the swamp road where the raptors take travellers and the garrison gets to them slowly.

She reaches them faster. The garrison has noticed and the quartermaster, apparently, has not.
background_sections.forward:
A ward. Four beds, a roof, and a place where somebody injured can lie down for a week instead of being patched up in a field.

She has found a building in Theramore and she has been negotiating for eleven months with a quartermaster who keeps asking whose authority she is under.

recruits.look: Colombian woman in her mid 40s, small and very upright, black hair in a severe low bun, a composed face that reveals nothing at all. Deep violet and black robes with a plain white collar, a slim dark staff, shadow pooling at the hem. A pair of folding reading glasses in a hard case, carried in one sleeve.

recruits.name: Diego Salazar
recruits.backstory: He fixed phones in a kiosk in Maracaibo from the age of fifteen, in a mall where the power went off twice a day and everybody had learned to keep working in the dark. He can take a thing apart faster than he can explain why. Of everyone who came through, he is one of the few who will say plainly that this world has been good to him, and he says it without apology, because the one he left had already stopped having anything for him.
recruits.greeting: Ah, you have a broken thing! Give it, give it. No, I am not guessing, I can hear it. Is the same sound every time, my friend.

background_sections.before:
A folding table, a tray of screws, and a queue.

Four older sisters, all of whom left the country in different years and different directions. He was the last one home and the one who stayed to look after their mother, and he was twenty-two when she died, eight months before the Integration.

So when it happened, he had nobody to lose. He has said that out loud exactly once, and then changed the subject to a gearbox.
background_sections.adjustment:
Three weeks, and he spent two of them delighted.

A goblin handed him a broken pressure valve to see what he would do with it. That is how a goblin asks a question. He had it working before the goblin finished the sentence and has been paid in parts ever since.
background_sections.forward:
A workshop with his name over the door, and he will tell you the exact sign he wants, in two colours, with the lettering slightly crooked because he likes it that way.

He is twenty-five and has never once been talked out of anything.
background_sections.now:
Wherever there is a pile of broken machinery and somebody willing to let him near it.

He has a half-built clockwork beetle that has been nearly finished for eleven months. Everybody who travels with him has been shown it. Nobody has seen it move.

recruits.look: Venezuelan man in his mid 20s, lean and wiry with quick hands, thick black hair falling over his forehead, dark eyes and a sharp jaw, a bright open good-looking face. Brass-and-canvas tinker's gear, a heavy wrench-hammer at his hip, goggles pushed up on his head. A phone-repair spudger, bright blue plastic scuffed white at the tip, in his breast pocket.

recruits.name: Freja Lindqvist
recruits.backstory: A midwife in Aarhus for six years. The job is being the calmest person in a room where something enormous is happening. She is matter-of-fact to the point of bluntness and people find it a relief inside about a minute. The Light came to her easily and she regards that as a tool rather than a calling, and she is careful to say so, because she has met two people here who got the other idea about themselves and she did not care for either of them.
recruits.greeting: Sit. You're bleeding and you're talking, and you can only do one of those well at a time. I'll tell you when you can start again.

background_sections.before:
Night shifts, a bicycle, and a flat with too many plants in it.

Her parents are alive and were in Aarhus. She has not found them. She has found the Danish lists at two hubs and neither one is complete, and she has decided to treat that as good news for as long as she can stand to.
background_sections.adjustment:
Steady, on the outside, from the first week.

What she had was a working pair of hands and a world full of people who needed them, and she used that the way you use a railing. She knows exactly what she was doing. She would do it again and recommends it to nobody.
background_sections.forward:
She wants to deliver a baby here. She has said this to three people and watched all three of them fail to understand why it matters to her.

Six years of her life were about the first ninety seconds of somebody else's. She would like to find out whether that still works in a place with this much dying in it.
background_sections.now:
Walking a circuit of the farms and camps, because the fighting gets a healer and the births get whoever is nearest.

She has taught four women to do what she does with their hands when she is not there. That is the part of the work she is proudest of and the part nobody asks her about.

recruits.look: Danish woman in her late 20s, tall and slim with a dancer's posture, long pale blonde hair braided back, grey-blue eyes, fine straight features. White and soft-gold priest robes with a pale blue mantle, a slim silver censer at the belt. A midwife's wooden pinard horn, polished dark with handling, at her side.

recruits.name: Sondre Haugen
recruits.backstory: He taught sailing to teenagers on the Hardangerfjord for four summers and expected to do a fifth. He is good with weather, good with boats, and he was twenty-four and had never had anything bad happen to him. Then the sky here started answering when he spoke to it, and the first time it went wrong it went very wrong, and he has been frightened of himself ever since. He is polite about it. You can still see it.
recruits.greeting: If I say get down, get down. Don't ask. The asking is the part that kills people, I have seen it.

background_sections.before:
A dinghy, a whistle, a clipboard, and a season that ended in August.

His family are in Bergen and he has no idea whether that means anything now. He describes them in the present tense, deliberately, every time, like a man holding a door open with his foot.
background_sections.adjustment:
He will say the first year was fine. Anybody who was there will tell you it was not.

There was an afternoon in the second year when the wind did something he had not asked for and a barn went over with people inside it. Nobody died. He has not been the same since and he has never been able to explain why, given that nobody died.
background_sections.forward:
Control. Not power. He has plenty of power and it is the whole problem.

He has started going out alone to practise where there is nothing to break. The people who care about him regard that as the worst possible way to handle this, and they are probably right.
background_sections.now:
The high open ground, where he can see weather coming for an hour before it arrives.

He sleeps badly. He is first awake every morning and has made the fire before anybody else is up. He offers this as proof that he is fine.

recruits.look: Norwegian man in his late 20s, tall and rangy with broad flat shoulders, dark blond hair pushed back and wind-wrecked, pale grey eyes, a weather-reddened face. Storm-blue layered robes with a short cloak that lifts on its own, a long bone-white stave, faint static along his forearms. A sailing-dinghy shackle key on a lanyard at his throat.

recruits.name: Berat Yilmaz
recruits.backstory: A dentist in Izmir, newly qualified, still paying for the chair when the world changed under him. The job is small careful work inside a space the size of a fist, on a person who would rather be anywhere else. That turns out to be most of what field medicine asks for. He is enormously good company and he knows it and he uses it, because a frightened patient is a patient who moves.
recruits.greeting: Open your mouth. No no, I am joking, I am joking! Old habit. Sit down, let me see the arm.

background_sections.before:
A surgery with his name on the door for eleven months, and a loan with thirty years left on it.

An enormous family, all of them in Izmir, all of them loud. He says he will find them. He says it the way you say a thing you have decided to believe, and he says it still, three years on.
background_sections.adjustment:
Two months, and most of that was the language.

He arrived with better hands than almost anybody and no idea what to do with the rest of himself, so he started asking everyone he met what they used to be. He now knows the former profession of roughly four hundred transplants and will introduce any two of them who ought to meet.
background_sections.forward:
A proper surgery again, with a door and his name on it, and an apprentice who is frightened of nothing.

He is also quietly assembling a list of every transplant with medical training, because he noticed early that nobody was keeping one, and it is now the only such list that exists.
background_sections.now:
Wherever the road is busiest, because that is where the broken arms are.

He still carries the mouth mirror behind his ear. He has used it twice for its actual purpose and perhaps forty times to see round a corner.

recruits.look: Turkish man in his late 20s, compact and sturdy, dark curls cut close at the sides, heavy black brows, warm brown eyes, an open face that smiles easily. Copper-plated tinker's coat in oxblood and brass, a backpack of tubes and gauges leaking soft green healing light. A dentist's angled chrome mouth mirror tucked behind one ear.

recruits.name: Matías Fuentes
recruits.backstory: He worked the Santiago buses from nineteen, punching tickets on a route he could have driven blindfolded, in a job his father had before him and thought was beneath him. What he is good at is standing still in a crowd of strangers for nine hours and watching all of them at once. He speaks carefully and not much, in an English he is still building, and people mistake that for stupidity about twice before they stop.
recruits.greeting: I go in front. Is better. You talk to me after, if you want. Now is not the time for talking.

background_sections.before:
A route, a fare box, and the same forty faces every morning.

His father died in 2019 and they had not spoken in two years. His mother and his brother were in Santiago. He does not talk about any of this and has told exactly one person, at night, while on watch.
background_sections.adjustment:
Bad. Very bad, and he will say so plainly if asked directly. Almost nobody asks.

He stopped speaking for most of the first year. Not deliberately. He simply ran out of things that were worth the effort of translating, and the quiet got comfortable, and then it got difficult to leave.
background_sections.forward:
He is learning to read this world's script, slowly, from a woman in a trade post who charges him nothing and corrects him constantly.

He has not told anybody why. The reason is that he wants to write a letter, and he knows there is nowhere to send it, and he wants to write it anyway.
background_sections.now:
At the front, because that is where you can see everybody.

He carries the ticket punch and clicks it twice before a fight, every time. Somebody asked him once whether it was for luck. He said no and did not explain.

recruits.look: Chilean man in his late 20s, slim and hard through the shoulders, black hair worn a little long and shoved back, dark eyes, high cheekbones. Charcoal and bone-grey reaper leathers with a hooded half-cape, a long curved scythe-blade carried low, faint violet light at the edge. A bus conductor's brass ticket punch on a cord at his belt.

recruits.name: Giorgi Beridze
recruits.backstory: Twenty years of high summer pasture above Kazbegi, moving sheep up and down a mountain on a calendar his family never wrote down because nobody needed to. He is physically enormous and completely unhurried. His English is small and he uses every word of it deliberately, and what comes out is often better than what a fluent man would have said, because he has no spare words to hide behind.
recruits.greeting: You walk too fast for the ground. Slow. The mountain will wait and so will you, if you listen.

background_sections.before:
A dog, a herd, a wooden hut, and six months a year without a road.

A wife, Nino, and two daughters in the village below, who he came down to every autumn and who thought the mountain was an eccentricity he would grow out of.
background_sections.adjustment:
Two seasons, and he counts in seasons.

The land here needed reading and he reads land. What took longer was people: on the mountain he spoke to nobody for weeks and that was normal, and here being alone is something others worry about on your behalf. He finds that exhausting and touching at the same time.
background_sections.forward:
A herd. He is serious and nobody takes him seriously. It irritates him more than he lets on.

He has found grazing he says is as good as anything at home, and a tauren who has begun to argue with him about it. He enjoys this enormously.
background_sections.now:
The high country, where the air is right and the ground tells the truth.

Every autumn, on roughly the right day, he walks down to lower ground for no reason anyone can see. He has never explained it. He is bringing the herd down. There is no herd.

recruits.look: Georgian man in his mid 30s, big through the chest with heavy forearms, thick dark hair and a short full beard, deep-set hazel eyes. Green and tan hide over mail, a hand-carved totem stave across his back, a hawk's feather bound into it. A shepherd's small dented brass bell, knotted to his belt so it cannot ring.

recruits.name: Camille Roussel
recruits.backstory: She was a bike courier in Lyon for nine years and a bicycle mechanic for all of them. The job is knowing exactly how much space you have and taking all of it. She is abrasive on purpose, fast, extremely funny when she decides to be, and almost nobody gets past the first layer. The ones who do find out that she is loyal to a degree she would deny under torture.
recruits.greeting: You want me to come. Fine. But I don't do the thing where we all talk about our feelings at the fire, yes? Good. We understand each other.

background_sections.before:
A fixed-gear frame she built twice, a radio in one ear, and a city she could cross in twenty-two minutes.

Her brother Théo rode for the same company. He was on the Part-Dieu road that morning and she was not, because she had swapped a shift. She has said this out loud twice and regretted it both times.
background_sections.adjustment:
She made herself useful immediately and let nobody near her for two years.

It worked, in the sense that she survived it. She is aware it was not the only option. She says the other options were for people with more patience than her.
background_sections.forward:
She has been mapping the roads between the camps, every one of them, by hand, by riding them.

Ask why and she says somebody should. The real answer is that it is the only thing she has found here that feels the same as the job did, and the job was the last part of her life that worked.
background_sections.now:
On the roads, carrying things between places faster than they have any right to arrive.

She will not take a message she has not read. She found that out the hard way in her second month and has been insufferable about it ever since.

recruits.look: French woman in her early 30s, slim and long-legged, dark brown hair in a thick loose plait over one shoulder, green eyes, elegant features and a faint knowing half-smile. Deep green and oxblood brigand leathers cut close, a hooded short cloak, a long dagger at the hip. A slim silver bicycle-spoke wrench threaded onto her belt.

recruits.name: Orlando Rivera
recruits.backstory: He cut hair in Santurce for eleven years in a shop that was really a front for the neighbourhood's entire social life, where everybody told him everything because a barber is a priest with better gossip. He talks constantly and listens harder than anybody notices. The spirits took to him immediately and he treats them the way he treated his chair: sit down, tell me what is wrong, I am going to fix it and we are going to talk the whole time.
recruits.greeting: Siéntate, siéntate. Okay, English. SIT. You look terrible and I say that with love, my friend, with love.

background_sections.before:
Two chairs, a radio always on, and a Tuesday regular called Don Beni who came in for nineteen years and never once needed a haircut.

His whole family were on the island. He says they are fine. He has a reason he believes this and he will tell you the reason and the reason is thin, and everybody lets him have it.
background_sections.adjustment:
He was running a chair inside a month, in a tent, with a borrowed blade.

It is the single most effective adjustment anybody made, and the reason is simple: he rebuilt the room. Everything he had on Earth came from having a place where people sat down and talked, so he made one here before he worried about anything else.
background_sections.forward:
A shop. Properly, with a floor and a mirror.

He has the blade. He has had three offers of a building. He has turned all three down and cannot explain why to anybody including himself, and his hands shook on the last one.
background_sections.now:
Wherever the party stops. That place becomes a shop for as long as they are there.

He will cut anybody's hair, any race, free, and he has never been refused twice by the same person.

recruits.look: Puerto Rican man in his early 30s, broad-shouldered and trim, black hair in a short fade, warm brown skin, an easy infectious grin. Bone and indigo witch doctor's gear, feathers and carved charms at the shoulder, a mask pushed up onto his forehead, a gourd rattle at his belt. A barber's pearl-handled straight razor in a sleeve pocket.

recruits.name: Adrián Mendoza
recruits.backstory: A football referee in the Segunda División for eight years, and before that a PE teacher. Two careers of being the least popular person on a field full of people. He is formal, exact and genuinely kind, and the formality is armour he put on so young that he has stopped noticing it. Give him a rule and he will hold it against everybody including himself, and he is the only man in any party who will tell you honestly when you were in the wrong.
recruits.greeting: Tell me the plan once, properly, and I will not ask again. I am not being difficult. I am being useful.

background_sections.before:
Twelve years refereeing in the Segunda División, and before that nine in regional football, which he will tell you was harder.

He lived in Valladolid, in a flat above a cycle shop, and the noise never bothered him. His parents died within a year of each other when he was twenty-eight. No brothers, no sisters. The friendships thinned out the way they do when you work every Saturday and half of Sunday, and he did not chase them.

He says all this the way he would read out a team sheet. Then he asks what you wanted to know.
background_sections.adjustment:
He was useful inside a week, which he found embarrassing.

The first thing he did here was reorganise a supply tent nobody had asked him to touch, and the second was argue with a quartermaster about it for twenty minutes. He won. He has been winning small arguments like that ever since, and apologising for none of them.

What he does not have a reference point for is being wanted in a room. In Valladolid the job was to be ignored. If he was doing it right, nobody said his name all afternoon.
background_sections.now:
Front line, holding whatever line he has been given, which turns out to be close enough to the old job that he is good at it immediately.

He gives the plan once. If you make him give it twice he will, and he will not be pleasant about it. Tarek has pointed out that he could simply be nicer. Adrián said he could, and did not.

He still carries the whistle. It is in the left pocket, always the left, and he pats it when he is thinking. He has never blown it here and would be mortified if anyone noticed how often he checks.
background_sections.forward:
He wants to be invited to something.

He is invited to everything. People come and get him — for meals, for watches, for the stupid card game Ama runs — and he goes every time and enjoys himself. But he has never once walked up to a fire and sat down at it without someone waving him over first, and after three years he still waits for the wave.

If you asked him about it he would say he does not want to intrude. He would believe it.

recruits.look: Spanish man in his early 30s, tall and square-shouldered, black hair cut short, close dark beard, a strong jaw. Polished steel and ivory templar plate with a deep red tabard, a one-handed sword and a shield at his back, faint gold light at the seams. A referee's whistle on a black lanyard inside the collar.

recruits.name: Saoirse Ni Bhraonain
recruits.backstory: She played county camogie until her knee went at twenty-six and then coached it. The sport is running at people holding a stick and expecting to be run at in return. She is loud, funny, and completely without self-pity, and she has an instinct for getting in front of things that predates any of this. Of all of them she is the one most people would want beside them, and she would find that embarrassing and change the subject.
recruits.greeting: Get behind me and stay there. I know, I know, you're very capable. Humour me and we'll both be alive to argue about it later.

background_sections.before:
A pitch in Kilkenny, a knee that clicked, and a minibus full of fifteen-year-olds she drove to matches at seven in the morning.

No partner, no children, two parents who had died within a year of each other, and a brother in Australia she spoke to twice a year out of habit rather than warmth.

The honest version, given without drama: there was nobody whose absence reorganised her. She says the girls on the team are the ones she thinks about.
background_sections.adjustment:
Easy, and she is a little ashamed of how easy.

She arrived into a world that wanted somebody to stand in front, and standing in front is the only thing she has ever been unambiguously good at. She has watched people far better than her fall apart while she got on with it, and she has no explanation and offers none.
background_sections.forward:
She wants to coach again. Not fight. Coach.

She has started with four of the Sentinels' youngest, on the grounds that somebody has to teach them to fall properly, and she runs it at seven in the morning because that is apparently who she is.
background_sections.now:
Wherever the shield wall is thinnest, taking the hits with a cheerfulness that other people find unsettling.

The sliotar is still on her belt. She throws it at people who are getting above themselves, underarm and accurately, and the party has learned to catch.

recruits.look: Irish woman in her early 30s, tall and strongly built, long copper-red hair tied back in a heavy knot, pale freckled skin, grey-green eyes. Silver and midnight-blue plate, a round shield with a crescent boss, a short spear, cold moonlight along the armour edges. A hurling sliotar, scuffed and grass-stained, in a net at her belt.

recruits.name: Nicolás Arce
recruits.backstory: Nine years a paramedic in Lima, mostly on motorbikes, because an ambulance cannot get through that traffic and a bike can. The work is triage at speed with your hands in somebody's blood, and blood magic asked him for exactly that with the pretence removed. He is steady, unhurried and very hard to frighten, and the one thing that will shut him down completely is being told to leave somebody behind.
recruits.greeting: Stand behind me. If I go down, you run, you do not drag me. Promise me this now or find somebody else.

background_sections.before:
A bike, a bag, and a city that produced more work than any crew could finish.

His partner on the bike for six years was called Rosa Quispe. She trained him, she swore at him constantly, and she was two streets away when it happened and he was not. He has looked for her at every hub he has reached. He keeps the list of hubs he has not reached yet.
background_sections.adjustment:
He worked. That is the entire answer and he gives it in those words.

The second year was worse than the first, because by then he had run out of places nearby to check and had to admit that the looking was going to be a long project rather than a short one.
background_sections.forward:
Rosa, obviously. He will not pretend otherwise and he will not make anybody else carry it.

Beyond that he wants a crew. Two people on a fast thing, going toward what everybody else is going away from. He has not found the second person.
background_sections.now:
At the front of the party, soaking what is aimed at the people behind him.

He is the one who notices an hour before anybody else that somebody is not right. He has never once announced it. He just ends up walking beside them.

recruits.look: Peruvian man in his early 30s, compact and visibly strong, black hair swept back, dark eyes, high cheekbones. Crimson and black plate worn heavy, a broad shield, a short thick blade, dull red light moving under the plate like something circulating. A paramedic's folding tourniquet windlass clipped at his shoulder.

recruits.name: Ileana Dragomir
recruits.backstory: Second violin in a Cluj orchestra for eleven years. The job is being corrected in public by a man with a stick and then doing it exactly right forever after. She is scathing about anything done carelessly and has no patience at all for effort without precision. She is also the first person on her feet when somebody goes down, every time, without comment, and the party worked that out long before she admitted it.
recruits.greeting: That was sloppy and you know it was sloppy. Do it again properly and I will stop talking about it. Probably.

background_sections.before:
A section, a stand partner, and the particular hell of being very good at something that has four hundred people better.

A husband, Andrei, who taught at the conservatory, and no children by a decision they made together and both revisited privately.

They had had a bad year and were coming out the other side of it. She describes the year in detail and the coming-out in one sentence, and the one sentence is the part she cannot say twice.
background_sections.adjustment:
Two years of being unbearable, by her own account, delivered flatly.

She is precise about her own faults in a way almost nobody is. She drove people off, she knew she was doing it while she did it, and she has apologised to four of them individually since and been surprised each time that it was accepted.
background_sections.forward:
She wants an ensemble. Not an audience. Three or four people who can hold a line while she holds hers.

She has said this once, in a way that made it clear she meant the party, and then immediately criticised somebody's footwork so that nobody could respond to it.
background_sections.now:
At the back, where the cold comes off her in a way the front rank has learned to stand clear of.

The shoulder rest is strapped across her back. There is no violin. Nobody has asked her about it twice.

recruits.look: Romanian woman in her mid 30s, slender and very upright, dark brown hair cut in a sharp chin-length bob, pale skin, dark eyes, fine sculpted features. Frost-white and deep grey robes with a high collar, a staff of pale bound bone, breath fogging and rime creeping along her sleeves. A violinist's black curved shoulder rest strapped flat across her back.

recruits.name: Thiago Macedo
recruits.backstory: A physiotherapist in Belo Horizonte who worked mostly with people recovering badly from things. The work is being relentlessly encouraging to somebody who wants to give up and is entitled to. He is huge, gentle and very hard to discourage. The Light came to him in the second year and the people who know him best say it did not change him at all, and he agrees, and finds that funny.
recruits.greeting: Hey, hey. Look at me. You are not dying today, this I promise you, and I do not promise things.

background_sections.before:
A clinic, a table, and a schedule of people he saw twice a week for months at a time.

A large family, all nearby, all in and out of each other's houses. He talks about them constantly and in the present tense, and he is one of the few who has had actual news: a cousin's name on a list at a hub in the south, eleven months ago. He has been walking south in stages ever since, and he is in no hurry, because he has decided it is certain.
background_sections.adjustment:
Eight months, and he spent them being useful to people in a way that nobody had asked for.

He was the man who sat with transplants in the bad weeks, before anybody organised anything. He still is. He does not frame it as a vocation and gets uncomfortable when others do.
background_sections.forward:
South, eventually, at his own pace.

He has also been teaching four people how to move an injured body without making it worse, because he watched somebody's back get broken twice: once by a boar and once by the people carrying him away from the boar.
background_sections.now:
In the middle of the party, where he can reach either end of it.

The roll of blue tape is nearly finished. He rations it. He has strapped three people's knees with it and he will tell you their names.

recruits.look: Brazilian man in his early 30s, tall and powerfully built, black curls cropped close, warm brown skin, a broad open face with a ready smile. Gold and white paladin plate worn light at the shoulder, a warhammer carried head-down, a soft gold glow around his gauntlets. A physiotherapist's half-used roll of bright blue kinesiology tape in a belt pouch.

recruits.name: Skye Donnelly
recruits.backstory: Eleven seasons with a Country Fire Authority brigade outside Ballarat. It is volunteer work that eats your entire summer and most of your friendships. She knows fire as a thing that has moods, and she is the only caster most people have met who treats her own magic as something to be managed rather than owned. She is very funny and swears a great deal and is completely dependable at the moment it matters.
recruits.greeting: Right, stand upwind and don't touch anything that's glowing. That's the whole briefing. You'll be fine.

background_sections.before:
A tanker, a pager, and a shed with a kettle in it where the crew sat out the nights nothing happened.

Divorced at twenty-nine, amicably, and she will say the fire brigade was most of the reason and that she would do it again. Her parents had retired to Queensland. She assumes they are fine on grounds she admits are entirely vibes.
background_sections.adjustment:
She found a fire in her first week and put it out, and says that sorted her head out for a year.

The harder part was discovering she could start one. She has thought about that more than she lets on and has a rule she tells nobody, and she has never broken it.
background_sections.forward:
A brigade. Actual volunteers, actual training, actual kit, for a world that burns constantly and has nobody organised about it.

She has six people. Four of them turn up. She describes this as going extremely well and she means it.
background_sections.now:
Out where the burning is, so in this world, most places.

The helmet torch is still clipped to her belt and the battery died two and a half years ago. She clicks it on sometimes out of habit and laughs at herself every time.

recruits.look: Australian woman in her early 30s, athletic and sun-browned, long honey-blonde hair pulled up messily, light blue eyes, freckles. Scorched orange and ash robes cut short at the sleeve, a slim rod wrapped in blackened wire, heat shimmer off her forearms. A firefighter's yellow smoke-stained helmet torch clipped at her belt.

recruits.name: Vuk Jovanović
recruits.backstory: He ran a kafana in Novi Sad that his uncle left him, and he is a far better cook than he is a fighter. He says so himself, with some bitterness. He is blunt to the point of rudeness about small things and completely reliable about large ones. He took to this world badly and is only now coming out of it, and the coming out looks like him feeding people and insulting them while he does it.
recruits.greeting: You cook this? Is terrible. Sit, I show you. No, sit. Is faster if I do it.

background_sections.before:
A kitchen, a card table, and forty regulars who came for the beans and stayed because there was nowhere else.

A daughter, Mila, who was nine, and an ex-wife he was on decent terms with. They had Mila on alternate weeks. It was not his week.
background_sections.adjustment:
Two years that he describes in three words and nobody presses him on.

What brought him back was being handed a cooking pot in a camp and being too irritated by how badly it was being used to leave it alone. He has been cooking for whoever is nearby ever since and he still says he is not a cook any more.
background_sections.forward:
He will not say. He has been asked and he changes the subject, every time, usually to food.

What is observable: he has started keeping a second bowl ready at every meal without being able to say who he thinks it is for.
background_sections.now:
At the front with an axe, badly, and at the fire afterwards doing the thing he is actually good at.

He carries a domino from the kafana set, the double six, in his glove. He puts it on the table when he sits down to eat. He has never explained this and nobody asks.

recruits.look: Serbian man in his mid 30s, very tall and heavy-framed, dark hair shaved close at the sides, pale eyes, an old thin scar through one brow. Black and dull-iron war plate with a torn dark surcoat, a two-handed axe across his back, faint cold green light in the gorget. A cast-iron domino tile, double six, carried in one glove.

recruits.name: Khalid Al Suwaidi
recruits.backstory: He kept falcons outside Al Ain, in a family that had done it for longer than anybody had written down, and he worked in logistics at the airport to pay for it. The hunting is the part of his old life that transferred whole: the waiting, the reading of ground, and the particular relationship with an animal that is choosing to come back to you. He is dry, extremely funny once you know him, and more at home here than he ever admits in company.
recruits.greeting: Walk where I walk and we will have a very boring day. That is the aim. Boring is the aim, I cannot stress this enough.

background_sections.before:
A mews, a glove, and a bird called Hurra who was eleven years old and who he had flown since she was a fledgling.

A large family, all nearby, all of whom thought the falcons were an expensive eccentricity and all of whom came out to watch anyway.
background_sections.adjustment:
Three months, and he has the grace to find it funny.

He came through into open country with weather and birds in it and no airport, and he says that if he is honest the first year was the best he had had in a decade. He says this quietly and only to people he has decided will not misunderstand it.
background_sections.forward:
A bird. Properly trained, properly flown, not a summoned thing.

He has been working on a nest of something enormous in the hills for two seasons, patiently, badly, and it has twice taken food from his hand and twice tried to remove it.
background_sections.now:
Out ahead of the party, usually invisible, always exactly where he said he would be.

The falconer's hood still hangs at his belt. It is sized for a bird that has been dead or alive for three years without him knowing which, and he will not be getting another one that size.

recruits.look: Emirati man in his mid 30s, tall and lean, black hair under a loosely wrapped cloth headscarf, close beard, dark eyes, a hawkish face. Sand, grey and deep red survival leathers with a short cloak, a long recurve bow and a heavy belt knife, traps and cord at his hip. A falconer's small tooled leather hood hanging from his belt.

recruits.name: Karim Haddad
recruits.backstory: A land surveyor out of Amman, fifteen years of standing in empty country deciding where the lines went, mostly alone and entirely content with it. He took the fel deliberately, after consideration, as the fastest route to being useful in a fight, and he will defend that choice in detail to anybody who raises it. He is cold on first meeting and very dry once he decides you are staying.
recruits.greeting: You are looking at the eyes. Everybody looks at the eyes. Ask the question or stop looking, either is better than this.

background_sections.before:
A tripod, a plumb bob, and weeks at a time in country with nobody in it.

No wife, no children, by preference rather than circumstance. His mother had died three years before, his father long before that, and his brother had moved to Canada in 2011 and they had slowly stopped calling.

He will tell you this flatly and without inviting any particular response, because he has noticed that people want to be sad on his behalf and he finds it tiring.
background_sections.adjustment:
He treated it as a survey. A new country, an unmapped one, and a man whose whole trade is deciding where things are.

He was functioning inside a month and has said more than once that having nobody to grieve made it easy, and that he is aware of how that sounds, and that it is still true.
background_sections.forward:
A map. The real one, properly surveyed, of how this world and the old one are stitched together, because the transit hubs make no sense and nobody competent has looked.

He is four years of work into something that needs twenty. He says so without any sign of minding.
background_sections.now:
Holding ground at the front, where the green light makes the people behind him uncomfortable and he has stopped apologising for it.

The plumb bob still hangs at his hip. He uses it. The party has learned that when he stops and lets it swing, something ahead is wrong.

recruits.look: Jordanian man in his mid 30s, tall and lean-muscled, black hair cut short, close-trimmed beard, dark eyes with a faint green cast. Dark iron and fel-green plate with heavy pauldrons, a jagged greatsword across the back, green light bleeding from the joints. A surveyor's brass plumb bob on a worn cord at his hip.

recruits.name: Osvaldo Beltrán
recruits.backstory: He played trumpet in a Havana hotel band for sixteen years, six nights a week, for tourists who talked through all of it. He is enormously talented at a thing nobody here has any use for, and that is most of what is wrong with him. He speaks little English and has made no particular effort to improve it, and he is blunt to the point of rude and has never once been unkind about anything that mattered.
recruits.greeting: You want fire, I give you fire. You want conversation, is the wrong man. Ask the Italian, he never stops.

background_sections.before:
A bandstand, a residency, and a brother on piano who was better than him and knew it.

His mother was ninety-one and lived three streets from the hotel. He went every afternoon before the set. He has said one sentence about her in three years.
background_sections.adjustment:
He stopped playing. There was nothing to play and nobody to play with, and he put it down, and it stayed down.

The fire came after that, and he will tell you the order matters. He was already empty when he went looking, and he thinks that is the only reason it took.
background_sections.forward:
Nothing he will admit to.

What is observable: he has twice stayed up all night with people who were in a bad way, saying almost nothing, just sitting there. Both of them have told somebody about it. He has denied it both times.
background_sections.now:
At the back, doing the loud part, with a flat expression that unsettles people until they get used to it.

The mouthpiece hangs at his throat. He has never been seen to use it. Somebody heard him humming once, badly, and had the sense to say nothing.

recruits.look: Cuban man in his late 30s, broad-chested and thick-armed, black hair shaved close, warm brown skin, a heavy-browed face that rarely moves. Scorched black and ember-orange robes with the sleeves burned back, a staff capped in a slowly burning coal, soot on his hands. A trumpet mouthpiece, brass gone dull gold, on a cord round his neck.

recruits.name: Bashir Khalidi
recruits.backstory: A stonemason in Nablus for twenty-two years, in a trade of taking something apart correctly before you rebuild it. He is severe, literal and entirely without small talk, and people read that as coldness for about a week. He hunts corrupted things the way he cut stone: slowly, along the grain, with no interest at all in how long it takes.
recruits.greeting: I will tell you what I find. All of it, including the parts you would rather I kept to myself. If that is a problem, say so now.

background_sections.before:
A yard, a chisel, and walls that his grandfather had worked on before him.

A daughter, Rana, nineteen, who had just started at the university in Birzeit and had told him the week before that she intended to study engineering rather than anything he had suggested. He had been pleased and had not said so yet.
background_sections.adjustment:
He went looking immediately and did not stop for eleven months.

He walked to four hubs in that time, on foot, through country that kills people. He found nothing. He came back, said nothing about it to anybody, and started doing the work he does now.
background_sections.forward:
He has never said. The closest anybody has got is that he keeps a list of places he has not searched, and the list is getting shorter, and he has begun to look at what is at the end of it.

He has told one person that he intends to be useful until then. That is the whole of the plan.
background_sections.now:
Out at the edge of the corruption with a lantern, where the work is slow and almost nobody volunteers.

He snaps the chalk line before he goes in anywhere. He has done it at every doorway for three years and he does it without appearing to notice he is doing it.

recruits.look: Palestinian man in his early 40s, tall and spare with long hard forearms, black hair cut short and grey at the temples, a severe face with a strong nose. Black and bleached-bone leathers under a long storm coat, a heavy crossbow at the hip, a silvered blade, a lantern burning pale white. A stonemason's blue-dusted chalk line reel at his belt.

recruits.name: Gianluca Ferri
recruits.backstory: He ran a bar in Bologna that his parents ran before him, opening at six for the people going to work and closing late for the people avoiding going home. Thirty years of standing behind a counter reading a room. He talks without stopping, he remembers what everybody drinks, and he has defused more fights with a joke than most soldiers have with a weapon. Behind the shield he is immovable and nobody expected that from the man who will not shut up.
recruits.greeting: You want to go in there? Fine, fine. But we go slow, and you let me go first, and afterwards you buy me something hot. This is the arrangement.

background_sections.before:
A counter, a machine he rebuilt himself twice, and the six o'clock crowd who never ordered because he already knew.

A wife, Ornella, who ran the kitchen and the money and most of him. Two sons, both grown and both in Milan, who rang on Sundays.
background_sections.adjustment:
He built a bar. Not a real one. A spot by a fire where he stood and people came to him, and he turned that into a job inside four months.

He has said that he did not know what else to do with himself, and that the thing he actually missed was not the bar, it was being the person everyone passes in the morning.
background_sections.forward:
A real one. A room, a door, a machine. He describes it constantly and in enormous detail and has done nothing concrete about it in three years.

He walks to the hubs every few months. He reads the Bologna list and the Milan list, in that order, and he reads the Milan list twice.
background_sections.now:
At the front of the party with a shield, where he keeps up a running commentary that the enemy finds as unsettling as everyone else does.

The brass tamper hangs at his belt. He has no coffee and no machine. He has been offered a dozen local substitutes and has tried all of them and rated every single one out of ten, unkindly.

recruits.look: Italian man in his late 30s, broad and solidly built, dark hair greying at the temples, close beard, brown eyes, a lined face that looks faintly amused. Burnished bronze and deep blue plate, a kite shield, a short stabbing sword, a furled banner behind one shoulder. A barista's brass coffee tamper, handle worn smooth, at his belt.

recruits.name: Elias Peralta
recruits.backstory: A motorcycle mechanic in Santo Domingo who went to church on Sundays because his grandmother expected it and stayed in the habit after she stopped being able to ask. He is the calmest person in most rooms. The Light arrived in his second year, during nothing in particular, while he was fixing a cart, and he has never once presented it as a sign. He treats it as a tool that showed up and he has been learning its tolerances ever since.
recruits.greeting: Take your time. I've got this side. Nothing's getting past me while you sort yourself out, hermano.

background_sections.before:
A workshop with a tin roof, four bikes in pieces at any time, and a radio he and his cousin argued over.

An enormous family in the capital and a girlfriend, Yamila, who he had been seeing for two years and had not told his mother about, for reasons that seemed important at the time.
background_sections.adjustment:
Slow and undramatic. He fixed things for about eighteen months and let everything else wait.

He will tell you he coped well and the people around him agree, and he has also said, once, that he thinks he simply has not got to it yet, and that it is still sitting somewhere waiting for him.
background_sections.forward:
He wants to build something that will outlast him, and he means a building, not a legacy.

He has drawn up a shelter for a crossing where travellers get caught out by weather. Four walls and a roof and a stove. He has shown the drawing to nobody, because he knows the first question will be who it is for and he does not have an answer that will satisfy anybody.
background_sections.now:
At the front, taking what is aimed at other people with an air of mild apology.

The inspection mirror lives in his gauntlet. He uses it to see round corners and, more often, to check on people behind him without turning round.

recruits.look: Dominican man in his early 30s, tall and lean with long limbs, black hair in a short twist-out, dark brown skin, warm dark eyes, a wide calm mouth. White and radiant gold plate with layered feathered pauldrons, a tall tower shield, light collecting above his shoulders. A mechanic's round telescoping inspection mirror in his gauntlet cuff.

recruits.name: Rui Almeida
recruits.backstory: He crewed a sardine boat out of Peniche from the age of sixteen, in a family trade that was collapsing under him the whole time he was in it. He is soft-spoken, apologetic and almost unbearably gentle, and he carries something that frightens him badly. He took it in his first year when the alternative was dying, and he has been paying for it since, and he has never once tried to make it sound like a good decision.
recruits.greeting: Please don't ask me what it is. I will tell you what it does and that has to be enough, because the rest I cannot say out loud.

background_sections.before:
Nights out and mornings in, a hold full of fish, and a co-operative that had gone from forty boats to nine in his working life.

His mother and his two sisters are in Peniche and he was the one who sent money. He thinks about that more than he thinks about them, and he knows that is a strange thing to be ashamed of, and he is ashamed of it anyway.
background_sections.adjustment:
Catastrophic. He was alone, he was hurt, and something offered.

He said yes. He has not defended that choice to anybody in three years. When people assume the obvious about him he lets them, because arguing would mean explaining, and explaining is the part he cannot do.
background_sections.forward:
Out. Quietly, without anybody making a fuss about it.

He has asked three priests and two shamans, carefully and in general terms, and nobody has given him an answer he believes. He keeps asking. It is the only thing he is stubborn about.
background_sections.now:
Behind the party, where he is extremely effective and visibly uncomfortable about it.

He sleeps nearest the fire. He has never said why and nobody has worked out that it is not the cold.

recruits.look: Portuguese man in his mid 30s, slim and a little gaunt, dark hair worn loose to the jaw, deep-set dark eyes, hollow cheeks. Deep violet and black robes with a torn high collar, a thin crooked staff, shadow pooling and moving wrongly around his feet. A fisherman's salt-bleached wooden net needle through his belt.

recruits.name: Nizar Haddad
recruits.backstory: He taught secondary-school mathematics in Homs for eleven years, then in Beirut for six, then in a language he was still learning for four more. He has rebuilt his life three times and this is simply the fourth, a fact he states without self-pity and which makes most transplants go quiet. His English is careful and faintly old-fashioned, learned from books and the BBC, and he is more precise in it than almost anybody born to it.
recruits.greeting: A moment, if you would permit me. I should like to understand the sequence before we add ourselves to it.

background_sections.before:
A blackboard, forty students, and the particular patience of a man explaining the same proof for the ninth time without letting it show.

His wife Lamia died in 2016, before any of the rest of it. His daughter Hala was twenty-two and studying in Amman and they spoke every single day, and he can tell you the time of the last call.
background_sections.adjustment:
Better than almost anyone, because he had done it before and knew the shape of it.

He has said that the first time you lose everything it destroys you, the second time it is merely very hard, and the third time you find you have a method. He does not offer this as wisdom. He offers it as information, to people who look like they need it.
background_sections.forward:
Hala. He is systematic about it in a way that is painful to watch: hub by hub, list by list, in a notebook, with dates.

He has also started teaching again, four children in a trade post, mathematics, in the evenings, for nothing. He says it is to keep his hand in.
background_sections.now:
At the back, holding the order of things together while the front rank does its work.

The broken watch runs backwards on its chain. He has never had it mended. He winds it every morning regardless and has not explained that to anybody.

recruits.look: Syrian man in his early 40s, tall and very upright, black hair greying at the sides, neat beard, dark eyes, deep laugh lines. Pale sand and deep teal robes with layered geometric trim, a staff of slowly counter-rotating brass rings, faint afterimages trailing his hands. A pocket watch with a cracked crystal, running backwards, on a fine chain.

recruits.name: Yusuf Al-Rawi
recruits.backstory: A pharmacist in Basra for nineteen years, in a shop where half the job was medicine and the other half was listening to people with no money for a doctor. He knows doses, he knows poisons, and he knows exactly how much of the truth a frightened person can take at once. He is enormously warm and completely unsentimental, and those two things together are rarer than either.
recruits.greeting: Sit, sit. You are not dying, I can see this from here. But you will sit anyway, because I am older than you and this is how it works.

background_sections.before:
A counter, a wall of drawers, and a queue that was also a social occasion.

A wife, Suhad, three sons and a daughter, and a house with too many people in it and a roof they sat on in the summer. He talks about them easily and often, in the present tense, and has never once been heard to speculate about where they are.
background_sections.adjustment:
Unhurried. He found the work and did it, the way he had found work in two other countries already.

He is one of the very few here who has said plainly that he expects to see his family again, and he says it so calmly that people believe him for as long as he is in the room.
background_sections.forward:
A dispensary. Shelves, drawers, labels, and somebody he has trained to run it when he is out.

He is also quietly teaching two people to read the labels he writes, because he has noticed that a dispensary nobody else can read is a dispensary that dies with him.
background_sections.now:
At the back with a bandolier of vials, dosing by eye and never once by guess.

The brass counting tray is strapped flat on his back. He uses it constantly. He is the only person in the party whose numbers are always right.

recruits.look: Iraqi man in his early 40s, broad and heavy-set but light on his feet, black hair receding and swept back, thick moustache and short beard. Dark green and gold robes with wide sleeves, a serpent-carved stave, corked vials in a bandolier across his chest. A pharmacist's scratched brass pill-counting tray slung flat at his back.
